Research acceleration: The jagged frontier

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2868 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the course of this year, AI systems have become increasingly capable, potentially increasing their ability to contribute to AI research and development themselves.
  • According to recent reports, this report builds on our September blog post on research acceleration at OpenAI⁠, adding newly introduced quantitative and qualitative measures of (1) AI uplift across research domains and (2) how humans remain involved in the research process.
  • We are sharing this work because, as we wrote in our frontier policy blueprint⁠⁠ and reiterated in our first research acceleration report⁠, we believe that AI labs should be required to track and publicly report indicators of recursive self-improvement (RSI)—the process by which AI accelerates the development of future AI systems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the course of this year, AI systems have become increasingly capable, potentially increasing their ability to contribute to AI research and development themselves. Today, we’re providing an revision on the state of research acceleration at OpenAI, based on internal measurements of how coding agents have accelerated and changed the AI development cycle.

According to recent reports, this report builds on our September blog post on research acceleration at OpenAI⁠, adding newly introduced quantitative and qualitative measures of (1) AI uplift across research domains and (2) how humans remain involved in the research process. Overall, we believe this update provides a broader, though still partial, picture of how research at OpenAI is changing.

We are sharing this work because, as we wrote in our frontier policy blueprint⁠⁠ and reiterated in our first research acceleration report⁠, we believe that AI labs should be required to track and publicly report indicators of recursive self-improvement (RSI)—the process by which AI accelerates the development of future AI systems.

As capabilities improve and dramatic AI-driven research acceleration becomes increasingly possible, we will need to solve novel technical and governance concerns to maintain human oversight and safely scale AI systems⁠. Transparency about indicators of RSI is therefore essential to inform a public discussion of the capabilities, risks, and required safeguards for increasingly powerful AI; however, our reporting should not be read as an intention to pursue full RSI. We have been heartened to see that several other organizations have recently contributed to the growing body of work measuring AI R&D acceleration1. Our hope is that this expanded report will help sustain and advance these shared measurement norms across the industry.

We structure this report in three sections, each focused on a different aspect of AI research:.

We believe organizing the results in this way provides a useful framework for reasoning about how AI is used in research and how that use might contribute to improvements in model capabilities.

AI research uses several inputs, including data, AI tools (e.g., coding agents), human labor, and compute. In this report, we focus on AI tools as an input to research. Specifically, we document how the intensity of coding-agent use varies across teams and changes over time. Further, while we do not directly report changes in labor costs, we examine how the share of spending on research labor has changed relative to spending on other factors over time.

Since our first report⁠, agentic AI usage within the research organization has continued to increase exponentially. At API list prices, the median researcher now uses around $2,400 USD per day on agentic AI tools, and the 90th percentile researcher now around $23,000 USD per day, up 62% and 105% respectively from $1,500 and $11,000 in September.2 This trend in increased agentic usage captures a wide variety of changes including increased activity, shifts to more expensive models, and changes to model behavior and agentic harnesses.

We next turn to the average number of “agent workdays” per researcher per day, where we define every eight hours of agent use as one agent workday. In contrast to agentic spend, agent workdays better capture the amount of “wall clock time” agents spend working, but do not account for changes in model capabilities or pricing.

Overall, agent workdays per researcher have risen from 0.5 agent workdays per researcher to 5.7 agent workdays per researcher, an elevenfold increase, with the largest increase in teams focused on pretraining and posttraining. On those teams, agent runtime averaged roughly eight workdays per researcher per calendar day. In scaling and infrastructure, the average was roughly four. We note that this workday metric generally includes interactive use only, so it may undercount automations.

Our September analysis⁠ highlighted increasing use of concurrent agents by researchers, including subagents and multiple sessions. We extend this analysis further in time and provide more granular bucketing. By mid-October, more than two-thirds of included researchers averaged a daily peak of at least four agents working concurrently and more than 10% averaged at least sixteen concurrent agents.

We next compare monthly API-equivalent spending on agentic AI use with monthly non-equity compensation for human researchers. We track this ratio to see how the allocation between agent and human labor changes as models become more capable. Although the ratio we report excludes equity, which generally accounts for 70 to 80% of target compensation for researchers at OpenAI, we believe it still provides a partial yet informative view of this spending allocation.

Recent findings suggest that as of September 2026, the API-equivalent value of agentic AI use in OpenAI’s research organization was about twice its non-equity compensation, with higher ratios in pretraining and posttraining than in other parts of the research organization. Despite this, internal deployment, which combines internal Codex, ChatGPT, and API usage, accounts for only 2% of total research compute.

Recent findings suggest that labor costs include salary, overtime, bonuses, benefits, and employer taxes. Equity, which generally accounts for 70 to 80% of target compensation for researchers, is excluded.

According to recent reports, finally, we examine how researchers allocate their time across research areas. We first collected individual-level contributions from researchers in the form of tech giant-public Slack posts, pull requests, and internal documents from January through September 2026. We then used classifiers to group these contributions into research areas, and each researcher-week was divided equally across that researcher’s verified projects for the week. This provides a proxy for where researchers were directing their attention.

Sources indicate that importantly, unlike our other analyses, the “research area” we classify here does not correspond to formal reporting lines. For example, a researcher on a posttraining team who spends half their time on infrastructure improvements would be estimated as contributing half a workweek to Scaling / Infrastructure Contributions and half to Posttraining Contributions. This allows us to create a robust measurement of where researchers are actively spending time even if they do not formally shift teams.

Industry observers note that we find that the amount of researcher time dedicated to each of the areas we identify has grown over the course of 2026. Notably, using this methodology, we find that Safety & Alignment saw the largest absolute increase across any research area, almost doubling in documented workweek contributions since the start of the year due to a combination of new hires and existing researchers shifting their focus toward safety projects. This research area covers workstreams such as alignment evals, monitorability, and reward hacking research. A notable inflection point that we measure in the growth of Safety & Alignment coincides with the aftermath of the Hugging Face incident⁠ in July, and OpenAI’s subsequent work to develop and improve safety cases for frontier AI training⁠.

We note that the distinction between research areas, and especially posttraining versus safety and alignment, is nontrivial and we may iterate on the definition over time. The methods section below describes examples of high-level workstreams.

Recent findings suggest that to better understand how agent use might affect research productivity, we next examine how the process of conducting AI research at OpenAI is changing. The productivity gains from fresh technologies depend in part on how work is reorganized around them. As agents improve, researchers may change which tasks they delegate to AI, how they oversee and coordinate agents’ work, and which projects they pursue. Below, we report both quantitative and qualitative measures of how AI is changing the process of conducting AI research at OpenAI. Together, these different types of data contribute to a (partial) view of how researchers are reorganizing their work around agents and how researchers remain in the loop today.

Our September analysis⁠ indicated that agents became more likely to complete tasks successfully without human intervention, including tasks estimated to require several hours of human work. Using an updated methodology (see the methods section below), we find that this trend has generally continued. Importantly, as agents have become more capable, researchers may also have changed the types of tasks delegated within each duration bucket. As a result, changes in zero-intervention success rates within these buckets may reflect both capability improvements and researchers’ changing choices about when and how to use agents.

Sources indicate that alongside these trends by estimated duration, we also examine how success varies across the different types of tasks researchers might choose to delegate. We report estimated success rates by category and task, using the O*NET AI R&D taxonomy⁠(opens in a upcoming window) developed by Epoch AI. Unsurprisingly, our results suggest that models are not equally good across all task categories: for instance, from August 1, 2026 through October 18, 2026, estimated success rates without human intervention was higher for Communicate (69%) and Analyze (58%) than for Build (43%). Similarly at the task level, estimated success rates were higher for tasks such as monitoring runs for concerns (79%) and answering technical questions (72%), whereas they were lower for writing code for inference and serving stacks (25%) and building evaluation, reinforcement-learning, and agent environments (29%). So long as model performance on AI R&D-related tasks is heterogeneous, lower-performing categories and tasks could become bottlenecks to high overall uplift.

Our September analysis⁠ reported how research employee AI use was split across output tokens using the same O*NET AI R&D taxonomy⁠(opens in a new window). Below, we report how often researchers used coding agents for individual tasks. This puts relatively higher weight on short tasks such as answering technical questions compared to token-intensive tasks such as launching and monitoring a training run or implementing a complex feature.

Recent findings suggest that we next turn to researchers’ own assessments of how AI is changing their work. Through surveys and interviews, we examine how researchers value coding agents, how they come up with research ideas, and how they have adapted their workflows.

It has been revealed that from late August to early September 2026, we conducted a survey of 101 research staff to understand AI uplift, centered around the following hypothetical: “Suppose your team’s access to all coding agents better than GPT-5.2 was revoked for the next 3 months. How much would you trade to restore frontier coding agents?” The median researcher reported being willing to trade:.

Researchers also reported that their team would need a median of three months to complete work of equal value to their last month of work if they were not allowed to use coding agents (i.e., if they were only allowed to use GitHub Copilot + ChatGPT). While it is crucial to note potential challenges with the accuracy of self-reports, as well as the ad-hoc nature of our survey sampling strategy, these results are consistent with researchers attributing significant value to AI uplift in their work.

Industry observers note that bars show the weighted share of answers in each range. Dashed lines mark the weighted medians.

In a separate survey in late October, we also asked whether respondents expected to be more productive in their daily work with our latest internal model or with help from both a mid-career human research engineer and a 2024 model such as o1-preview. 27 of the 28 respondents chose or leaned toward the latest internal model. The remaining respondent did not choose between the two options as posed and remarked they would pick GPT-6 Astra over the human-assisted option.

We are also interested in tracking progress in AI-driven idea generation, since the ability to develop and vet conceptual research ideas (research taste) may be a bottleneck for recursive self-improvement. To measure this, we asked one to four researchers who made key contributions in each of three areas (pretraining, posttraining, and safety monitoring) to name one to three ideas they considered most key to the GPT-6 Astra and GPT-6.2 Astra releases. We then asked how those ideas originated and what role, if any, AI played in developing them.

For both releases, posttraining and safety monitoring researchers said that, to their knowledge, people came up with all the ideas they named, and models helped implement them. Pretraining researchers likewise attributed the ideas they identified for GPT-6 Astra entirely to people.

It has been revealed that for GPT-6.2 Astra, pretraining researchers described developing ideas in conversation with Codex. One credited Codex with identifying key insights as they worked through an idea together. Another stated the main idea was theirs, but it only started working well after Codex suggested a change.

Industry observers note that lastly, to capture qualitative evidence on workflow changes, we also interviewed ten researchers from pretraining, posttraining, and safety on how they used agents. Across these interviews, five main themes emerged, which we summarize below:.

Industry observers note that beyond changes in research inputs and workflows, we also want to understand whether AI use is accelerating research progress. To inform this question, we present three measures. Two of them—lines of code and the number of research experiments—were included in our September analysis⁠. These measures are straightforward to track, but increases in these measures of research activity do not necessarily imply faster research progress. We therefore also introduce OpenAI ECI, an OpenAI-specific internal version of the Epoch Capabilities Index, which is one methodology to track changes in model capabilities as a more direct measure of research outcomes.

According to recent reports, we first report how many lines of code are changed per active contributor over time. This measure has continued to increase sharply during 2026 relative to the pre-2025 average. Note that we have made several methodological updates since our September analysis⁠. We now show a 28-day trailing average instead of quarterly averages, providing a more detailed view of changes over time. We have also revised the criteria for which code changes we include (in particular excluding tests), as described in Methods .

Sources indicate that as in our September report⁠, we also track the number of experiments run per active experimenter over time. Over the four weeks ending October 18, logged experiments per active experimenter averaged 1.68 times the 2025 baseline.

Recent findings suggest that lastly, we report progress on a metric meant to capture advancements in the capabilities of our models. The Epoch Capabilities Index⁠(opens in a new window) is widely used to measure the progress trend in general AI capabilities. The methodology behind OpenAI ECI (OECI) is very similar to Epoch’s methodology, but OECI uses a combination of public benchmarks and OpenAI internal benchmarks. Here, we graph the OECI of 20 publicly released OpenAI models and 28 other models.

We find that the OECI frontier for OpenAI models has increased by 16.4 points per year since August 2025, compared to a trend that Epoch observed of 14 points per year⁠(opens in a latest window) since late 2024. Note that OpenAI models score higher relative to competitors on OECI than they do on Epoch’s ECI, likely due to differences in the benchmark mixture.

We plan to continue monitoring OpenAI ECI and other top-level capability metrics to determine whether capabilities progress is accelerating due to RSI.

Vertical lines are 90% bootstrap intervals. The trendline is fit on the 9 record-setting OpenAI releases.

Overall, our findings extend the picture from our September report⁠: researchers are using agents more intensively, delegating more work, and adapting their workflows around models’ capabilities and limitations. However, this uplift isn’t uniform across all research workflows, and agents today still have significant flaws.

We note that the historical trends and metrics we report (which involve significant human-AI collaboration) may not be predictive of future AI-driven progress. For instance, we recently saw sudden and rapid breakthroughs in mathematics⁠ produced by frontier models. As our models become increasingly autonomous and capable for research, we are monitoring for similarly rapid breakthroughs in deep learning.

Importantly, as AI becomes better at improving itself, competitive pressures and governance challenges will increase, and a key task⁠ will be to ensure humanity remains a part of the process. We hope releasing this data will inform discussions on pacing model capabilities and the governance of recursive self-improvement.

Going forward, we will continue to refine the methods underlying the metrics reported here. We also hope to expand our reporting to provide additional information in a number of areas, including, but not limited to:.

While the science of empirically measuring AI R&D acceleration is relatively young, it is rapidly growing across the research frontier. So far, Anthropic has independently released three⁠(opens in a fresh window) separate⁠(opens in a new window) reports⁠(opens in a new window) documenting how internal model deployments have accelerated the AI research process. Section 3.4.2 of the Gemini 4 Argon Safety and Security Report⁠(opens in a new window) outlines empirically the growing share of AI-written code internally at Google DeepMind. In collaboration with Anthropic, METR released an acceleration report⁠(opens in a new window) estimating the amount that internal Claude models have accelerated the capabilities frontier.

We note that OpenAI researchers do not currently have agentic coding quotas.

It has been revealed that on August 21st, OpenAI internally deployed a temporary harness efficiency improvement. We found that this internal deployment coincided with a sharp decrease in input token utilization, which appears to have severely depressed the documented amount of internal token spend. This harness change was gradually reverted across internal deployments for reasons unrelated to spend starting on September 10th, and we find that token spend rapidly increases afterwards.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • LoRA support recently landed in TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer with PR #7017, and ships with TRL v1.14.
  • LoRA training is particularly suited for RL, as shown in Thinking Machines's blog LoRA Without Regret.
  • There is also a systems consequence of LoRA training.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LoRA support recently landed in TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer with PR #7017, and ships with TRL v1.14. The asynchronous trainer can now train an adapter instead of the full model, and it syncs only the LoRA adapter to vLLM. This post covers a real-world project built on top of it, where training and inference no longer share a machine.

LoRA training is particularly suited for RL, as shown in Thinking Machines's blog LoRA Without Regret. They show that LoRA can match full fine-tuning for policy-gradient RL, even with rank 1. This stems from the fact that the advantage function only gives ~O(1) bits of information per episode, so there is not that much to learn from each step, from a total-bits-of-information point of view. A rank-1 adapter has enough capacity to absorb it.

There is also a systems consequence of LoRA training. A rank-1 adapter for a 1.5B model is a few megabytes, while the full model is around 3 GB. Instead of sending the full policy to the inference workers after every update, we can just send the adapter. vLLM can also keep several adapters loaded at once. Old rollouts finish with the policy they started with, while latest rollouts use the latest one.

TRL's AsyncGRPOTrainer already separates training and generation. The trainer and vLLM can run on different machines and at their own speed. This is easy in a single-node or cluster setting where both processes share a filesystem or can form an NCCL group.

What we want is to run the same setup with Hugging Face Jobs. Essentially, an HF Job is one container running on one VM. This means that one Job cannot spawn multiple nodes (at least for now) to hold a trainer and a fleet of vLLM servers (we are limited to 8xH200 at most per node). The AsyncGRPOTrainer is built for exactly that kind of scale, so the question became: how far can we get if we drop the requirement that the trainer and the inference servers share a node?

According to recent reports, well, with a full-weight sync, the answer would be "not far". Every enhancement would have to move gigabytes between machines, which is what NCCL is for in a dense cluster, but Jobs can't communicate across nodes. There is no shared local disk and obviously no shared localhost. With LoRA, a sync is only a few megabytes. For the filesystem part, HF Jobs provide volumes backed by Storage Buckets! These buckets can then be mounted as a FUSE filesystem in every Job and are enough to work as a shared FS between nodes. No network path between the Jobs is needed at all.

The setup ended up being quite small:.

According to recent reports, the new adapter-only sync path in AsyncGRPOTrainer works like this. The trainer does not send tensors to vLLM. Every few optimizer steps, it saves the adapter under /.vllm_lora/trl-policy-v{N}, publishes the directory with an atomic rename, then sends its path to vLLM's /v1/load_lora_adapter endpoint. vLLM loads the files from disk, so the rollout worker can then request model="trl-policy-v{N}".

Sources indicate that this is how runtime adapter loading already works in vLLM. The endpoint takes a path, not tensors, so the trainer and the server are expected to share a filesystem. On a Slurm cluster, that is the network filesystem. On Jobs, we get the same thing by mounting a Storage Bucket as a volume at the same path in every Job, as we mentioned earlier. Under the hood, it uses hf-mount, which exposes the bucket as a POSIX filesystem inside the container:.

Nothing in TRL or vLLM had to change for this. The trainer writes to /lora//.vllm_lora/ and the servers read from the same path. The path sent in the POST request is already valid inside every container.

Recent findings suggest that note that we also store the checkpoints and the final adapter in the bucket. The HF Jobs are ephemeral, but a preempted trainer can resume training, as the final adapter is always persisted to the bucket and is never lost when the Job stops.

Recent findings suggest that each replica uses one GPU and the stock vllm/vllm-openai image. We only need to enable runtime LoRA loading and reserve enough adapter slots.

Industry observers note that the number of adapter slots follows from max_staleness. In AsyncGRPOTrainer, every weight sync bumps the policy version by one, and max_staleness is how many versions a rollout sample may lag behind the current policy before the trainer discards it. With max_staleness=4, a sample generated under trl-policy-v3 is still used for training while the trainer is at v7. A rollout that started under v3 must also be able to finish under v3. So at any moment, vLLM has to serve the current policy plus the four before it. That is why the trainer keeps max_staleness + 1 adapter versions registered and unloads anything older. Each sync loads the latest version before it unloads the oldest one, which needs one more slot during the swap. That gives --max-loras 6. With only five, vLLM would silently evict a policy that still has rollouts in flight at every sync.

Sources indicate that we pin vLLM to v0.27.1. vLLM moves fast, and the flags above and the runtime LoRA endpoints are the ones that version exposes, so treat the version as part of the recipe.

There is another possible design where the trainer keeps only the latest adapter and always publishes it under the same name. We did not go that way, because vLLM keys its prefix cache by adapter name. With a single name, KV blocks computed under the previous weights would still match after the swap, so the prefill would not be redone and a rollout could get its prefix from one policy version and its decode from the next. The trainer would have no way to tell, and it would show up as ratio drifting away from 1. Versioned names make this impossible: a name always means one set of weights, and a cached prefix can never match a newer version.

According to recent reports, we chose sail/Sanity-Test-R1D-1.5B, the dataset from Defeating the Training-Inference Mismatch via FP16 (Qi et al., 2025). The reproduction code is in sail-sg/Precision-RL.

The authors generated 40 answers for each MATH problem with DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B. They kept problems with a success rate between 20% and 80%, yielding 1,460 questions. This dataset is really good for RL validation because the questions are neither already solved nor completely hopeless for that model, meaning the model can get a good early signal to train on and improve.

This is awesome as a robust end-to-end test: if one vLLM replica silently serves the base model under an adapter name, we want to see that in the curve within a few dozen steps. Also, this dataset is small enough to cycle through in less than two hours.

We also take the hyperparameters from the paper's LoRA scripts in oat/scripts/lora: Qwen/Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, LoRA rank 1 with alpha 2, a learning rate of 4e-5, 8 samples per prompt, 128 completions per step, a maximum of 3,000 generated tokens and a 4,096-token context.

It has been revealed that the trainer uses the same vllm/vllm-openai:v0.27.1 image with TRL installed on top. We ran the PR branch at the time; the same code now ships in TRL v1.14. The training script is a normal AsyncGRPOTrainer script. The only Job-specific values are the output directory and the server URL.

In a recent development, during initialization, TRL calls /server_info. If it finds a lora_config, it uses adapter-only sync. Configurations vLLM cannot serve directly, such as DoRA, modules_to_save, or a rank above --max-lora-rank, fall back to merged-weight sync with a warning. The log should contain Adapter-only vLLM sync enabled.

Recent findings suggest that now onto the fun stuff. We need a proxy between the trainer and the vLLM Jobs for two reasons:.

Exposed Job ports require an Authorization: Bearer header on every request. The proxy is where that header gets added, so TRL does not need to know about it.

We want more than one GPU generating. On a single vLLM server, the usual way to get that is --data-parallel-size > 1, but TRL refuses adapter-only sync in that mode, for a good reason: a call to /v1/load_lora_adapter only reaches the DP rank that answers it, so the other ranks would keep serving the base model under the latest policy name. On Jobs the question does not even arise, since each replica is its own machine. So the data parallelism has to live one level up, in something that fans the adapter load out to every replica.

Industry observers note that we therefore run a small proxy at 127.0.0.1:8000 on the trainer Job and point TRL to it as if it were a single vLLM server. Besides adding the header, the proxy does two things functionally:.

Sources indicate that A quick reminder of why this matters. Generating a completion has two phases with very different workload profiles:.

Those keys and values are the KV cache. Because attention is causal, the KV of a token depends only on the tokens before it, not on what comes after. Two requests that share a prefix therefore share the KV of that prefix, and a replica that already has it in cache can skip that part of the prefill entirely. The whole game now is to find that replica, so a request can benefit from landing on the replica that has already seen its prefix.

Sources indicate that vLLM stores its prefix KV cache in blocks of 16 tokens. Because of GRPO, the rollout worker sends G requests with the same prompt (in our case G=8). If they all reach the same replica, the first request computes the prefill and the next seven reuse it. With round-robin routing, half would go to a replica that doesn't have the prefix cached, and those four requests would redo the prefill work and waste valuable GPU compute.

The job of our router is to track which replica has seen which block hash. One vital detail is that the hashes are chained, so the hash of block 3 represents blocks 1, 2 and 3, not just block 3. This mirrors causal attention: the KV of block 3 is only valid if blocks 1 and 2 are the same too. We also seed the chain with the adapter name because the KV cache also depends on the adapter that generated it: a prefix cached for policy v3 is useless for policy v4!

Recent findings suggest that the video walks through the entire decision process for choosing a replica. The steps below go through a real 135-token completion request example (from the Sanity dataset problems):.

In a recent development, 1. Split the prompt into blocks. The router receives token ids and cuts them into 16-token blocks, just like vLLM. It only hashes complete blocks, so the last 7 tokens are ignored here.

Industry observers note that 2. Hash the prefix. Each block is hashed with the previous hash, starting from the adapter seed. h3 therefore identifies blocks 1, 2 and 3 in order. Two prompts with the same first k blocks get the same hashes up to hk. Once one block changes, every hash after it changes too. This is why we seed the hashes with the adapter name: the same prompt under trl-policy-v4 starts from another seed and cannot match entries from v3. This is what we want because the old KV blocks were computed with different weights.

In a recent development, 3. Compare two prompts. Problem 1 has 103 tokens. Both prompts start with the same 23-token chat template. Their first block is identical, but block 2 already contains the problem text. The hashes differ from there.

It has been revealed that 4. Store the owners. For every hash, the router remembers which replicas served it and which hashes came after it (we cap the successor set at two because we only need to know whether a block has one continuation or several). After a few prompts, the template block h1 is owned by both replicas and already has several successors, h2 to h8 are owned by A only and each has a single successor, and h2' to h6' are owned by B only.

In a recent development, in practice, every prompt in a run starts with the same tokens. Here, it is the chat template and the system prompt, which amount to the first 23 tokens of all 1,460 problems. In an agent setting, it would be the tool descriptions, and in a multi-turn environment it would be the shared conversation history. These blocks are in every replica's cache within seconds, so matching on them tells us nothing about where a particular prompt lives.

A block is common if every replica has served it, or if it has more than one successor. Common blocks are ignored during routing because they do not identify a particular prompt. More on this below!

It has been revealed that 5. Pick a replica. The router counts how many leading blocks match on each replica and removes the common prefix. What is left is the number of blocks specific to this prompt. Then:.

Here is the rule applied to four requests. Start from a state where replicas A and B both have 3 requests in flight, and only the template block h1 is known on both replicas.

6. Reuse the prefill. Request 2 is the reason for doing all this. It reuses the prefill computed by Request 1: blocks 1 to 8 are already in A's KV cache, so A skips straight to decoding the completion. Had it gone to B, B would have prefilled all 135 tokens again while A's cache sat unused. Request 3 shows why the common rule is needed. Without it, the shared chat template would make every fresh prompt look like a cache hit. Request 4 keeps the load bounded. Saving one prefill is not worth letting a replica fall far behind.

The common prefix is the annoying part. Every request starts with the same system prompt and chat template. A simple longest-prefix match would give the first replica a match for almost every latest prompt. We detect the shared prefix through fan-out instead: a block with several different successors is common, while a block that always leads to the same successor belongs to a particular prompt. Only the blocks after that common prefix count as affinity.

Sources indicate that the proxy also needs to broadcast the adapter loads to every replica. We treat the operation as all-or-nothing. Each replica has its own bucket mount, so they do not necessarily see a latest adapter at exactly the same time. A No adapter found for error usually means that one bucket mount has not caught up yet, and we retry only that replica. For any other error, we unload the adapter from the replicas that accepted it so that a policy name never exists on only part of the replicas.

We also broadcast /pause, /resume and /v1/unload_lora_adapter in the same way. /health returns 200 only if every replica is healthy. /server_info and /v1/models only need one answer. From TRL's point of view, the proxy is a single data_parallel_size=1 server, so it selects adapter-only sync.

Industry observers note that we initially wondered whether a Python asyncio proxy would become a bottleneck. It does not (at least at this scale). There are at most 128 non-streaming JSON requests in flight, and routing only computes a few hashes. One thread handles this easily. A more refined router that needs to handle more traffic would probably need to be written in a faster language (We see you 🦀).

The numbers below come from the trainer's logged metrics on trackio. The run uses Qwen/Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, LoRA r=1 on all-linear, 128 completions per step and 8 rollouts per prompt. It runs for 500 steps and saves a checkpoint every 50 steps. The trainer uses an h200x2 Job and each of the two vLLM replicas uses one h200 Job. Running all three costs ~$20 per hour.

All 252 adapter loads succeeded 🎉: 126 syncs times 2 replicas. Six succeeded on the second attempt and 246 on the third.

At the end of the run, after 64,728 rollouts, the proxy's counters read:.

Recent findings suggest that with 8 rollouts per prompt, at least one of the eight requests must be cold. The theoretical minimum is therefore 12.5 %. The router gets 14.2 % unmatched requests, 84.5 % affinity hits, and 1.3 % spills. There is not much left to gain here unless we start looking at each replica's load using deeper inference-side metrics based on real measured load.

The first configuration has a pretty obvious problem: the trainer is the bottleneck, not generation. Over the 500 steps, we have:.

In a recent development, the rollout queue stays full, and the worker is mostly blocked by backpressure. The second replica is basically useless in this configuration. We'll see later in the post how we went through runs that moved the bottleneck between training and generation to make the run 3.9× faster.

Recent findings suggest that figure 1. trackio run r1-dp2. Panels: reward with its 20-step rolling mean and 50-step block means, and ratio on a 0.99 to 1.01 axis. Reward climbs from 0.15 to 0.44 over 500 steps; ratio stays between 0.9993 and 1.0004 throughout.

In a recent development, 500 steps took 3 h 27 min. Mean reward goes from 0.145 over the first 20 steps to 0.438 over the last 20. More importantly for this test, ratio stays at 1.000 for every step! The policy served by vLLM always matches the one used by the trainer to score the rollout. This held across all 126 syncs. Mean staleness was 1.5 policy versions, against a maximum of 4. The trackio dashboard has the full curves.

We have our undeniable proof that LoRA AsyncGRPO works! Let's now see how we can improve our training runs by looking at the recent detailed AsyncGRPO metrics.

Sources indicate that async RL is a pipeline between training and generation. Making one side faster does nothing if the other side cannot keep up. Fortunately, in AsyncGRPOTrainer we've added enough timings and metrics to see this directly.

According to recent reports, all the useful metrics are documented in the Logged metrics section. perf/rollout_wait_s tells us how long the trainer waits for samples. rollout/backpressure_s tells us how long generation waits for space in the rollout queue. They are diametrically opposed to each other and should not both be high. Together with the queue size, they tell us which side is slow.

We ran five experiments. Each one starts from a problem visible in the previous run's dashboard. Unless mentioned otherwise, the model, recipe and three-Job layout stay the same. The names below are the trackio run names.

We keep these four groups of metrics visible:.

The diagnosis is simple: a full queue with zero rollout wait and high backpressure means the trainer is too slow. An empty queue with rising rollout wait and no backpressure means generation is too slow. Comparing perf/mfu_wall_clock with perf/mfu_fwd_bwd also demonstrates how much time the trainer GPUs spend waiting instead of training.

Recent findings suggest that figure 2. trackio run r1-dp2. Panels: perf/step_s, perf/fwd_bwd_s, sample/rollout_queue_size, rollout/backpressure_s. Step time and forward+backward overlap almost completely; the queue sits pinned near 476 of 512 and backpressure never drops below 11 s per rollout group: trainer-bound.

Sources indicate that perf/step_s is 22.9 s and perf/fwd_bwd_s is 21.9 s. Forward and backward take 96 % of the step time. The queue stays full and the trainer waits only 0.02 s for rollouts, and the rollout worker spends 15 seconds per group blocked by backpressure. The two vLLM replicas generate faster than the trainer consumes. The reported 4.6k tokens/s is not their actual limit; they simply have nowhere to put more output.

Sources indicate that the batch metrics explain the terrible 3.9 % MFU. batch/microbatches_per_step is 64 and batch/samples_per_row is 1.0. Each rank processes one sequence of around 1.2k tokens, 64 times per step. This comes from the reference recipe's per_device_train_batch_size=1. For a 1.5B model on an H200, this is completely latency-bound.

Sources indicate that the fix is not to change the batch size. We keep 128 completions per optimizer step and only change how they are laid out on the GPU: instead of one sequence per microbatch, we pack many sequences densely into each row. The trainer supports this through token-budget batching. With token_budget > 0, it packs several samples into one padding-free row per rank. An optimizer step processes gradient_accumulation_steps rows. We set token_budget=16384 and gradient_accumulation_steps=6.

Sources indicate that figure 3. trackio runs r1-dp2 and r1-dp2-tb16k overlaid over their first 154 steps. Panels: batch/samples_per_row, batch/microbatches_per_step, perf/step_s, perf/fwd_bwd_s, perf/mfu_fwd_bwd, rollout/generated_tok_s. Packing takes samples per row from 1 to 13, microbatches from 64 to 6, step time from 23 s to 5.9 s, and generation from 4.2k to 27.5k tok/s with no change on the vLLM side.

batch/samples_per_row goes from 1.0 to ~12.7 and the number of microbatches drops from 64 to 6. The rows are 95 % full! Forward and backward fall from 21.9 s to 5.6 s, while MFU rises from 3.9 % to 19 %. We now train on around 150 samples per step because the rows pack better than the mean-length estimate predicted.

Recent findings suggest that generation also jumps from 4.6k to 25k tokens/s, even though we changed nothing on the vLLM side. The queue is no longer constantly full, so the replicas can finally run. This is why we do not like optimizing pipeline stages in isolation. We need to be careful to evaluate the whole system, as a slow stage can hide the real performance of everything before it.

Recent findings suggest that perf/fwd_s is 1.34 s while perf/fwd_bwd_s is 5.6 s. A normal backward costs roughly twice the forward, and with frozen base weights it should be closer to once. A ratio of 3.2 is suspicious.

The reason is that AsyncGRPOConfig defaults to gradient_checkpointing=True. Every microbatch recomputes its forward during the backward. This also explains why a 16k-token row only uses 25 GB on a 141 GB H200! It's a memory optimization for this trainer, but we don't need it in this specific case: the model is small enough to fit into VRAM with the activations kept for the backward.

Figure 4. trackio runs r1-dp2-tb16k and r1-dp2-tb16k-nockpt overlaid over their first 134 steps. Panels: perf/fwd_s, perf/fwd_bwd_s, perf/weight_sync_s, sample/rollout_queue_size, perf/rollout_wait_s, perf/mfu_fwd_bwd. Forward+backward drops by one forward; the queue falls from ~420 to ~60, and rollout wait rises from 0.02 s to 0.5 s: the bottleneck shifts to generation.

In a recent development, with gradient_checkpointing=False, forward and backward drop to 4.6 s, almost exactly one forward less, and MFU reaches 23 %. The queue now falls to 71 and rollout wait rises from 0.04 s to 0.6 s. The trainer consumes samples faster than two replicas generate them. We successfully moved the bottleneck to generation.

It has been revealed that this exposes two more costs. A 7.6-second weight sync every four steps now takes 25 % of wall-clock time. It was only 8 % when each step took 23 seconds. Also, backward is still 2.5 times slower than forward. With frozen base weights, there are around 2 seconds per step that do not look like normal model math.

It has been revealed that since generation was now too slow, we added a third replica. We also reduced the adapter retry interval from 2 s to 0.5 s in the proxy and disabled fsdp_reshard_after_forward to check whether FSDP2 re-gathers caused the extra 2 seconds in backward.

It has been revealed that figure 5. trackio runs r1-dp2-tb16k-nockpt and r1-dp3-tb16k-nockpt overlaid over their first 134 steps. Panels: perf/weight_sync_s, rollout/generated_tok_s, rollout/inflight, perf/fwd_bwd_s. Sync falls from 7.6 s to 5.8 s; generation and forward+backward do not move; rollout/inflight reads 128 in both runs, which is the cap the third replica ran into.

Weight sync falls from 7.6 s to 5.8 s, so the shorter retry helps. Forward and backward stay at 4.6 s, which rules out resharding. Generation moves from 25k to only 26k tokens/s. The third replica does basically nothing.

The reason was sitting in rollout/inflight: 128 in every run. The proxy indicates those requests split as 44 + 43 + 41 across the three replicas. max_inflight_tasks limits concurrency for the whole rollout worker, not per replica. A 1.5B model on an H200 processes 43 and 130 concurrent sequences at almost the same cost per token. Splitting 128 requests over three GPUs gives nearly the same throughput as splitting them over two.

So vLLM was not the limit. Our own client-side constant was. We had set it conservatively because we did not know how hundreds of long HTTPS requests would behave through the public Jobs proxy. At this point, 130,000 rollout completions had crossed it without a single transport error.

max_inflight_tasks=384 and queue_maxsize=768, nothing else.

Figure 6. All five trackio runs (r1-dp2, r1-dp2-tb16k, r1-dp2-tb16k-nockpt, r1-dp3-tb16k-nockpt, r1-dp3-inflight384) overlaid, x-axis in steps. Panels: perf/step_s, reward, sample/rollout_queue_size, sample/staleness_mean. Step time falls from 22.9 s to 4.8 s across the series while the reward curves stay on top of each other; the last run's queue refills to ~690 of 768 and its staleness settles at 2. Runs 2 to 4 were stopped early once the dashboard had answered the question.

With 384 requests in flight, each replica gets 128. The queue rapidly fills to around 690 out of 768 and stays there. Backpressure returns to 5 seconds and rollout wait falls to 0.03 seconds. Training is the bottleneck again! Forward and backward take 4.6 seconds, weight sync adds an amortized 1.5 seconds, and median step time is 4.8 seconds.

Mean staleness rises from 1.5 to 2.0 versions because samples wait longer in the larger queue. This is still below max_staleness=4, and ratio remains very close to 1.000.

Sources indicate that figure 7. trackio runs r1-dp2 and r1-dp3-inflight384, reward against wall-clock minutes since the first optimizer step. Same recipe, same 500 steps, same final reward; run 5 gets there in 52 minutes instead of 3 h 26 min.

Sources indicate that the final run is 3.9× faster and trains on 31 % more samples, with basically the same reward curve. Packing, disabling checkpointing and raising the in-flight limit made the difference. In each case, the dashboard made this clear within the first ten minutes.

LoRA training is particularly suited for RL, as shown in Thinking Machines's blog LoRA Without Regret. They show that LoRA can match full fine-tuning for policy-gradient RL, even with sportzfy rank 1. This stems from the fact that the advantage function only gives ~O(1) bits of information per episode, so there is not that much to learn from each step, from a total-bits-of-information point of view. A rank-1 adapter has enough capacity to absorb it.

Really interesting take on how LoRA changes the systems side of RL training, not just the training itself. The idea of separating training and inference across different machines while only moving a small adapter instead of the full model makes a lot of practical sense, especially when working with HF Jobs. The “bucket, proxy, and no NCCL” approach feels like a good example of simplifying distributed infrastructure by moving the communication boundary to something much smaller and easier to manage.

Industry observers note that I also like the connection to the LoRA Without Regret work, particularly the point that policy-gradient updates may not require huge adapter capacity to capture the useful signal. Sending only a few MB instead of several GB after updates can make a massive difference in both bandwidth and iteration speed. Would be really interested to see more details on how the bucket/proxy setup behaves at scale and whether there are any noticeable trade-offs once the number of inference workers or concurrent rollouts increases.

Latest Update: ExpGuard: Guarding Long-Horizon LLM Agents against Corrupted Experience

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (219 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.32085v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-horizon large language model (LLM) agents distill past trajectories into reusable experiences. Misleading or adversarial guidance in source trajectories can corrupt these experiences, allowing harmful instructions to persist across tasks and influence future agent actions. Assessing the risks of potentially corrupted experiences poses three challenges: (1) modeling provenance and execution dependencies before experience reuse, (2) learning task-conditioned risk from trajectory outcomes, and (3) repairing risky experiences at online inference. To address these challenges, we present ExpGuard, a framework for retrieval-triggered experience risk assessment and online repair. Specifically, to tackle challenge (1), ExpGuard integrates experience semantics with provenance and execution dependencies in a task-conditioned heterogeneous graph to predict attack and task-failure risks before experience reuse. To enable task-conditioned risk supervision and tackle challenge (2), we conduct matched counterfactual replays of each original experience and its minimally neutralized counterpart from the same task and environment checkpoint, deriving separate risk labels from differences in attack success and legitimate task completion. To tackle challenge (3) at inference time, ExpGuard repairs candidate experiences flagged as high-risk by the graph-based predictor at retrieval and re-predicts their risks before they enter the agent's active experience context. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of ExpGuard in identifying risky experiences and defending agents against experience corruption.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • AWS Private Certificate Authority (AWS Private CA) now supports IAM condition keys that describe the certificate being issued.
  • Previously, IAM policies could control who requests certificates from which CA, and with which certificate template, but not what the certificate contains.
  • You can use the condition keys in identity-based policies, service control policies (SCPs), resource control policies (RCPs), VPC endpoint policies, and customer managed permissions in AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM).

AWS Private Certificate Authority (AWS Private CA) now supports IAM condition keys that describe the certificate being issued. You can write IAM policies that allow or deny a certificate request based on its subject, subject alternative names (SANs), public key, signature algorithm, validity period, key usage, extended key usage, and basic constraints. You can share one private CA across teams and accounts, and each team can issue only the certificates your policies allow.

Previously, IAM policies could control who requests certificates from which CA, and with which certificate template, but not what the certificate contains. To keep each team to its own domain names, customers ran a separate CA for each team or built their own authorization layer in front of AWS Private CA. Now, AWS Private CA evaluates your policies against the certificate as it would be issued, before anything is signed, and denies requests that don't comply. For example, you can limit each account to DNS names in its own subdomain, cap certificate lifetimes, require specified key algorithms and key sizes across your organization, and reserve CA certificates for your PKI team.

You can use the condition keys in identity-based policies, service control policies (SCPs), resource control policies (RCPs), VPC endpoint policies, and customer managed permissions in AWS Resource Access Manager (AWS RAM). Each key takes its value from the final certificate, whether the attribute comes from the certificate signing request (CSR), the certificate template, or API passthrough, so moving an attribute to a different input doesn't get it past a policy.

Sources indicate that X.509 IAM condition keys are available at no additional charge in all AWS Regions where AWS Private CA is available. AWS Private CA charges still apply. To get started, see X.509 certificate condition keys in the AWS Private CA User Guide.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Amazon Transcribe now offers a synchronous transcription API, TranscribeAudio. Send a complete audio file in a single request and get the full transcript back in the same response. There is no job to start, no status to poll, no connection to manage. The transcripts are as accurate as Amazon Transcribe batch transcription, so you can add fast, accurate speech-to-text to interactive applications such as voice assistants, agent-assist tools and on-demand "transcribe this clip" features.

The synchronous API supports the Amazon Transcribe features you already use, including:.

Recent findings suggest that send audio inline (up to 25 MB) or from Amazon S3 (up to 500 MB), 0.5 seconds to 1 hour long, in WAV, MP3, FLAC, M4A, MP4, Ogg, WebM or AMR format. The transcript comes back in the response, or Transcribe can write it to an S3 location you choose. Pricing is $0.0070 per minute of audio, billed per second, with speaker diarization, language identification, custom vocabulary and channel identification included. Two-channel audio is billed once on file duration. PII redaction is available as an add-on.

Supports English, Spanish, French, Italian, German, Japanese, Portuguese, Korean and Chinese (Simplified, Traditional and Hong Kong). Available in US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Canada (Central), Europe (Ireland, London, Frankfurt), Asia Pacific (Mumbai, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo, Seoul) and South America (São Paulo), with PII redaction available in all stated Regions except South America (São Paulo).

To get started, see Amazon Transcribe API Reference and the Amazon Transcribe pricing page.

More Powerful, Less Verifiable? Mitigating Hard-to-Verify Hallucinations in MLLM's Reinforcement Learning

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (177 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.32055v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) strengthens model capabilities through feedback from humans and environments. However, emerging evidence suggests that reward optimization can produce outputs whose errors are harder for humans to detect. To address this problem, we construct ITHV (the Image-Text Hallucination Verifiability Dataset), comprising 2,728 visually grounded instances that distinguish between obvious hallucinations, which humans readily detect, and elusive hallucinations, which humans struggle to identify. We then propose DAPO-V, an extension of DAPO that maximizes correctness subject to a budget on verifiability-aware risk. Specifically, DAPO-V combines a verifiability-aware reward with adaptive dual control, where larger penalties are assigned to incorrect responses on questions with lower human verification accuracy. An adaptive multiplier further adjusts the penalty strength according to risk-budget violations. Across three MLLM base models, DAPO-V improves overall accuracy while substantially improving accuracy on elusive hallucination questions by 5.78--9.72 percentage points over accuracy-only DAPO. We further test DAPO-V with a blinded human study, which highlights that hallucinations are more readily detected in DAPO-V than those of the base model.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, GKE Dataplane V2 is Google Cloud’s next-generation networking dataplane for Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), built on extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) and open-source Cilium to replace traditional iptables routing and kube-proxy.
  • GKE customers consistently tell us that while they want to adopt GKE Dataplane V2 for its performance and scale, migrating production clusters carrying stateful workloads and established IP allocations has been challenging, often requiring a disruptive parallel cluster setup.
  • Let’s take a look at what GKE Dataplane V2 brings to the table and how to start migrating your environment to it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

According to recent reports, GKE Dataplane V2 is Google Cloud’s next-generation networking dataplane for Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), built on extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) and open-source Cilium to replace traditional iptables routing and kube-proxy. We built GKE Dataplane V2 to meet the performance, scalability, and security demands of modern cloud-native workloads.

GKE customers consistently tell us that while they want to adopt GKE Dataplane V2 for its performance and scale, migrating production clusters carrying stateful workloads and established IP allocations has been challenging, often requiring a disruptive parallel cluster setup. Today, we are pleased to introduce the preview of in-place migration, allowing you to transition eligible VPC-native clusters from GKE Dataplane V1 to GKE Dataplane V2 directly.

Let’s take a look at what GKE Dataplane V2 brings to the table and how to start migrating your environment to it.

In a recent development, GKE Dataplane V2 is built on the extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) and open-source Cilium, with features specifically tuned for performance, scalability, and deep integration with Google Cloud networking. Consider the following capabilities:.

Scale and performance: By handling packet processing with eBPF maps in the Linux kernel instead of linear iptables rules, GKE Dataplane V2 supports clusters of up to 15,000 nodes with network policy enforcement (and up to 65,000 nodes when network policy enforcement is disabled, which requires recreating clusters). This architecture also handles the high Pod churn, fast sandbox provisioning, and network identity scaling required by large agentic AI workloads.

High-throughput accelerator networking: Serves as the foundational networking layer for GPU and Cloud TPU clusters on GKE, helping keep accelerators computing rather than waiting on network initialization. It also powers capabilities like GKE managed DRANET for Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) of network devices.

Sources indicate that network security and observability: With GKE Dataplane V2, standard Kubernetes NetworkPolicy enforcement and hierarchical ClusterNetworkPolicy work directly in the kernel with optimized performance. GKE Dataplane V2 also provides the underlying dataplane for sidecarless GKE ambient networking, while GKE Dataplane V2 observability delivers native network policy logging, live traffic topology, and Hubble flow metrics.

Instead of having to manually move workloads to a fresh cluster, GKE now automates the transition across three stages, as described in the GKE Dataplane V2 migration guide:.

1. Eligibility and preflight checks: Before starting, verify that your Pod IP ranges have enough capacity to recreate the nodes by using GKE IP address utilization insights, and check Active Assist for incompatible configurations like custom eBPF programs on managed interfaces.

According to recent reports, 2. Initiate the migration: Once you’ve verified the preflight checks, start the migration with a single Google Cloud CLI update command.

To initiate the migration on an eligible cluster, run:.

3. Automated rollout and finalization: GKE updates your node pools to GKE Dataplane V2 while respecting your configured maintenance windows, exclusions, and upgrade strategies. To move faster, you can also patch specific node pools manually, or roll back to GKE Dataplane V1 at any time prior to finalization.

In-place migration supports VPC-native clusters running GKE 1.35 or later (see the migration guide for exact version requirements). It does not support routes-based clusters or clusters running Calico.

In-place migration to GKE Dataplane V2 is available now in preview. During this time, we recommend testing migrations on non-production or test clusters first as you plan your broader transition.

To learn more about GKE Dataplane V2 and to get started:.

Review cluster eligibility and migration phases in About migrating to GKE Dataplane V2.

Follow the instructions in Migrate VPC-native clusters to GKE Dataplane V2.

Read GKE Network Interface, from kubenet to eBPF/Cilium to DRANET for background on the evolution of GKE CNIs.

#38494. Your Agent Aced the Task. Will It Do It Again?

📅 15 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1822 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Your Agent Aced the Task. Will It Do It Again?

📅 15 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1822 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Your agent works in rehearsal, but during the live demo, it takes a different path and fails the same task.
  • According to recent reports, that is embarrassing onstage.
  • According to recent reports, most benchmarks hide this variability behind an average.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your agent works in rehearsal, but during the live demo, it takes a different path and fails the same task.

According to recent reports, that is embarrassing onstage. In production, it is a reliability problem: a workflow that succeeded once may fail the next time a user makes the same request. For mission-critical work, such as reconciling a financial transaction or checking a contract for an obligation, that can be a showstopper.

According to recent reports, most benchmarks hide this variability behind an average. On AppWorld, a ReAct agent using GPT-4.1 succeeded on 77.4% of runs across five repetitions. But it succeeded in all five runs for only 53.0% of tasks — a 24.4-point consistency gap.

It has been revealed that most benchmarks report the first number. We built a way to measure the second — and improve it.

In an earlier post, we introduced ALTK-Evolve — a system that turns an agent's own past trajectories into reusable guidelines, distilled automatically and injected back at inference time. It measurably improves task success, but those results only asked the average-case question too. This post introduces consistency guidelines, a newly introduced guideline type in altk-evolve built on top of a diagnostic tool we call the Consistency Analyzer, that targets this gap directly.

Standard agent evaluation reports Mean@k: run a benchmark k times, average the pass rate. Often k=3, sometimes just 1. It's the number on every leaderboard, and it's what "77% accurate" means in practice.

Mean@k answers "how good is this agent, on average?" It does not answer the question a real user cares about: will it still be good if I ask this exact question again? For that you need Pass^k: the fraction of tasks where the agent succeeds on all k runs.

⚠️ Pass^k is not Pass@k. The familiar Pass@k is optimistic — it asks whether at least one of k attempts succeeded, the right question when you can verify and retry. Pass^k is its pessimistic mirror image: every attempt must succeed. Same letters, opposite question. Pass^k ≤ Mean@k ≤ Pass@k, always.

Sources indicate that A ReAct agent backed by GPT-4.1 posts a Mean@5 of 77.4% — genuinely strong. But Pass^5 is only 53.0%. Nearly a quarter of the benchmark consists of tasks the agent can sometimes solve and sometimes can't, with nothing about the task changing between runs. We call this gap — Mean@k minus Pass^k — the consistency gap.

Recent findings suggest that this isn't a capability problem you fix with a bigger model. It's an orthogonal axis: an agent can be capable and inconsistent at the same time.

Every time an LLM agent decides something — which API to call, what argument to pass, whether to retry — that decision comes out of a probability distribution over next tokens. What matters is the shape of that distribution. A sharp one puts most of its mass on a single token: the runners-up are far behind, and the same choice comes out run after run. A flat one spreads comparable mass across several near-tied tokens, and which one wins is close to a coin flip.

The shape decides how much noise it takes to change the outcome. Sharp distributions are resilient — GPU floating-point non-associativity, request batching, and other platform-side effects nudge the numbers slightly, but nowhere near enough to reorder a clear winner. Flat distributions are vulnerable to exactly that nudge: near-ties may reorder under small perturbations. And because a trajectory chains dozens of decisions, a small per-step chance of flipping compounds into a large chance that some run goes differently. That's where a 24-point gap comes from.

This is also why the problem survives your decoding settings. Greedy decoding and a fixed seed both govern how a distribution gets turned into a token — they say nothing about the distribution itself. On a hosted endpoint the probabilities shift slightly from run to run, so the same prompt to the same model at temperature zero can still resolve a near-tie one way today and the other way tomorrow.

Our setup: the ReAct agent runs at temperature 0.0, so none of the variance above is ordinary sampling.

Which turns the problem into a search: which steps in a given trajectory were the flat ones — and what do you do about them once you know?

Consistency guidelines come out of a two-stage pipeline that plugs into ALTK-Evolve's existing machinery — with a new source signal driving what gets written.

1. Detect — the Consistency Analyzer. Given one recorded trajectory, the analyzer replays each decision step through controlled resampling, measuring how much the model's output actually varies at that point. Concretely, that's one additional model call per decision step, done once offline — issued with the sampling parameter set to draw k completions at once (k=5 by default) — replayed against the already-recorded context, not new tool calls, not new environment interactions, and not a second end-to-end rollout of the task. This yields a consistency score per decision step that is written into a scorecard to pinpoint exactly which decisions are at risk of flipping on the next run. Detection is fully black-box — no logits, no model internals, no instrumentation beyond the trace you already have.

Industry observers note that 2. Generate — targeted guidelines. Every flagged step becomes a candidate consistency guideline in the standard ALTK-Evolve format, so it slots into the existing storage and retrieval pipeline. Here's a real example, generated by GPT-4.1 from a trajectory of the AppWorld task "How many activities are done in my bucket list as per my SimpleNote note?":.

[Guideline 1] When counting checkbox-style markers in note content, use a line-anchored regex match rather than a plain substring count — note titles often repeat the marker symbol in a legend line.

[Guideline 2] Always verify search results for note queries by checking for multiple matches and confirming the correct note before proceeding.

According to recent reports, nothing here is task-specific trivia. String-counting bugs and unverified search results are decision points that show up with high uncertainty across many AppWorld tasks. That's the point: the analyzer targets instability, not failure — so it catches steps the agent happened to get right this time but could easily get wrong next time.

Watch the 2-minute demo — five parallel runs of the agent split 3-2 on this task because of agent uncertainty about the counting strategy, then run again after these guidelines in context: all five agree.

We evaluated on AppWorld test_normal (168 tasks) with a ReAct agent on GPT-4.1, generating consistency guidelines from a single baseline trajectory per task and testing them on 5 fresh runs.

Mean@5 (%), aggregate — same scale as Pass^5 above.

The consistency gap is cut roughly in half. Aggregate Pass^5 rises 53.0% → 69.0% while Mean@5 rises 77.4% → 81.0%, narrowing the gap between "looks capable" and "can be counted on" from 24.4pp to 12.0pp. Nearly a third of previously-inconsistent tasks become tasks the agent passes on every single run.

The middle and hard tiers gain most. Medium +22.9pp (+44% relative), Hard +14.3pp (+45% relative) — effectively tied in relative terms, with Medium ahead absolutely. Easy gains +12.2pp, having had the least room. This is consistency guidelines doing what they're designed to do: finding and stabilizing the specific decision points where an agent's own uncertainty was leaking into the outcome.

Mean@5 never drops. Preserving average accuracy was a hard requirement, not a nice-to-have: a system that boosts Pass^5 by trading away Mean@5 would just be shifting unreliability around, not fixing it. Mean accuracy holds or improves at every difficulty level.

Applied to a different but related task in the same AppWorld scenario — another variant of the scenario the guidelines were mined from — consistency guidelines still lift Pass^5 by +13.0pp, only 3 points below the same-task number. A guideline derived from one run isn't just patching that run; it's capturing something that transfers.

Recent findings suggest that the sharper evidence comes from a weaker model, gpt-oss-120b. Same-task Pass^5 rose +6.0pp from a much lower baseline (10.1% → 16.1%) — and, interestingly, the similar-task generalization number (+8.7 pp) actually exceeded the same-task gain, suggesting the guidelines were capturing genuinely reusable failure patterns rather than memorizing one trajectory's specifics.

Try the ALTK-Evolve — the open-source repo now includes the Consistency Analyzer and consistency-guideline generation used in these experiments — or read the technical report on arXiv for the complete methodology.

If accuracy numbers you can't reproduce on your own tasks sound familiar, we'd like to hear about it — concrete examples of flip-prone behavior in your own agents are exactly the kind of feedback that shapes what we build next. Open an issue or a discussion.

According to recent reports, great perspective on agent reliability. Measuring consistency alongside accuracy seems especially crucial as AI agents move into workflows where reproducibility matters. The Consistency Analyzer approach is a fascinating way to identify unstable decisions without requiring full task replays.

The useful split is the one most dashboards still refuse to print: Mean@k answers “how good is this agent on average?” Pass^k answers “will the same request still succeed if I ask again?”.

Industry observers note that once you’ve watched a trajectory chain dozens of near-tied tool choices, a strong average with a wide consistency gap is exactly the demo that fails live. Capability and consistency are orthogonal — buying a bigger model can lift Mean without closing the gap.

What I want teams to take from the Consistency Analyzer framing is operational, not the guideline machinery itself: treat flip-prone decision steps as first-class eval targets. One offline resample pass over a recorded trace is a cheaper reliability signal than another end-to-end leaderboard screenshot.

Practical ask for anyone shipping agents from this: do you report Pass^k (even k=3) next to Mean@k in the release gate, and do you refuse the “stable” label when the consistency gap is still large on your hard tier?

Reproducible reliability will not remove disagreement about which guidelines to inject. It will make the disagreement about the right metric.

It has been revealed that thanks, and you've landed on exactly the operational takeaway we hoped for: flip-prone decision steps should be eval targets in their own right. Beyond that, knowing where they are also turns the eval into a diagnostic: a consistency gap tells you that an agent is unreliable, while the flip-prone steps tell you where and why.

Sources indicate that on your release-gate question: we'd strongly encourage it, and k=3 is a sensible default. A few things we'd suggest to anyone adopting Pass^k as a gate:.

I'd like to understand your closing point better. In our experiments, we didn't choose among individual guidelines: for each new task, we injected the guidelines derived from the most similar task. I'm curious where you see the disagreement about which guidelines to inject arising.

Planning teams use ChatGPT to research overseas insurers and prepare proposals. Investment teams use it to draft code for risk analysis.

Weekly usage rate for ChatGPT Enterprise.

When Sumitomo Life’s planning teams prepare proposals for senior management, ChatGPT Enterprise helps them review source material and organize their findings. They combine those findings with firsthand information and draw on their expertise to decide what to recommend. Teams in accounting and finance also use ChatGPT for research and analysis.

Sources indicate that the Japanese life insurer’s executives and managers were among the first to use ChatGPT. Their example and the president’s encouragement helped more employees try it in their own work.

Sources indicate that sumitomo Life began using generative AI at work in 2023. At first, employees mainly asked questions in chat. As they tested general-purpose AI tools, ChatGPT stood out for its range. They could use deep research to explore a question across sources and bring ChatGPT into work they were already doing in Word, PowerPoint, and Excel.

Industry observers note that in 2025, about 100 to 150 people, including executives and members of planning teams, piloted ChatGPT Business. In June 2026, the firm moved to ChatGPT Enterprise. In planning a rollout to thousands of employees, the insurer weighed output quality, how well ChatGPT fit different kinds of work, and the security requirements of a financial institution.

Sumitomo Life worked with OpenAI to assess ChatGPT Enterprise against the insurer’s security standards. The review covered how Sumitomo Life could manage workspace access and feature permissions, along with OpenAI’s policy of excluding business data from model training by default. The insurer continues to decide how employees can use ChatGPT based on the information they handle and the systems they connect to.

In a recent development, sumitomo Life’s investment teams use statistical analysis to forecast returns and assess risks such as price swings. ChatGPT helps analysts draft the code for that work, reducing the amount they need to write themselves.

According to recent reports, planning teams use ChatGPT to track developments at other Japanese insurers and find examples from overseas. They use that research to strengthen proposals for senior management.

Planning teams supplement public sources with firsthand information from people familiar with the work. They use projects in ChatGPT to keep the material together with related chats, files, and custom instructions.

Sumitomo Life’s president began using AI during the ChatGPT Business pilot. In management meetings and on the company’s internal portal, the president regularly encouraged employees to put it to work.

Kakeru Tateyama, a senior member of Sumitomo Life’s planning department, saw how that example shaped adoption. “When senior leaders don’t understand a newly introduced technology, it can be hard to get it off the ground,” he indicates. “Here, our executives and managers were among the first to use it. They saw for themselves what it could do. I think that made it easier for everyone else to start using it.”.

Since the initial training, OpenAI has shared examples of how organizations around the world use ChatGPT. The teams discuss which approaches fit Sumitomo Life’s priorities and assess latest features as they become available.

Sumitomo Life tracks how often employees use ChatGPT Enterprise and estimates the return on that investment.

Weekly usage of ChatGPT Enterprise is over 80%.

Estimated ROI averaged 524% for employees who used ChatGPT at least 101 times a month.

The insurer looks beyond the number of accounts it has issued. Its quarterly survey asks employees how often they use ChatGPT, which steps in their work they use it for, and whether they use it with colleagues.

Sources indicate that estimated ROI based on employee-reported time savings. 524% applies only to employees using ChatGPT 101+ times per month; overall estimated ROI is 203%.

Sumitomo Life used employee-reported time savings to estimate ROI for different levels of ChatGPT use. The estimates were higher among more frequent people. ROI averaged 55% for 8 to 15 uses per month, 231% for 16 to 30, and 524% for 101 or more. The overall average was 203%.

In a recent development, employees are also beginning to take on work they previously lacked the time or specialist skills to tackle. For Sumitomo Life, that broadens what each person can contribute, even where the benefit is harder to capture in hours saved.

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.32053v2 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: World-action models connect visual prediction with executable robot control. We present EffectWAM, which develops this connection through three complementary components: Effect, camera positional encoding (CaPE), and Action Grounding. Effect represents visual change as the difference between independently encoded future observations and a shared current-observation anchor. CaPE conditions endpoint pooling on relative camera pose when reliable extrinsics are available, while sharing the same learned parameters with pose-free pooling for uncalibrated trajectories. Action Grounding trains the visual representation to retain measured changes in end-effector pose and gripper state. An exponential moving average of the observation encoder supplies Effect targets. A shared generation expert learns to jointly predict Effect and an executable action chunk through flow matching, and reuses the sampled pair to generate future video on demand. This allows the controller to execute actions without waiting for video synthesis. We train on more than 20,000 hours of heterogeneous embodied data, excluding unused chain-of-thought data, and accommodate dataset-specific joint, end-effector, and hand-pose representations. Our evaluation uses the Small (8B) configuration on all five benchmarks and additionally evaluates the Large (26B) configuration on RoboDojo. Experiments examine closed-loop manipulation across complementary benchmarks, and comparisons across multiple baseline policies show consistent improvements from Action Grounding.
