💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that ever wonder how the Google Ads team keeps the massive system stable and online, despite continuous attempts by hackers to take it down?
  • The Google Ads team uses a central graph-based platform to fight fraud and abuse with batch and real-time signals.
  • The need for a graph-based abuse detection platform stems from how the global threat landscape has evolved.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Director, Engineering, Google Ads.

Group Product Manager, Data Cloud.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

It has been revealed that ever wonder how the Google Ads team keeps the massive system stable and online, despite continuous attempts by hackers to take it down? Part of the answer is using Spanner as its core operational and graph database.

The Google Ads team uses a central graph-based platform to fight fraud and abuse with batch and real-time signals. Built to protect the Google Ads ecosystem and now used by multiple teams across Google, the platform organizes anti-abuse intelligence into a single, interconnected view. Its core mission is simple but critical: uncover hidden connections between malicious assets in real time before they can harm users or advertisers. This blog talks about the challenging modern fraud and abuse landscape, and how Spanner, specifically Spanner Graph, helps Google successfully detect those threats.

The need for a graph-based abuse detection platform stems from how the global threat landscape has evolved. Digital advertising fraud and online scams are no longer minor operational nuisances, they are a massive drain on the global economy. According to the NASDAQ Global Financial Crime Report, total global fraud losses are estimated at nearly $580 billion for 2025. Furthermore, global surveys indicate that approximately one in five adults fall victim to scams. In digital ads, fraud and abuse waste marketing spend, corrupt attribution data, and expose everyday consumers to financial scams, identity theft, and malware.

Bad actors are increasingly leveraging automation and AI to scale deceptive campaigns more efficiently. In 2025 alone, Google blocked or removed more than 8.3 billion policy-violating ads and suspended 24.9 million advertiser accounts. As these tactics evolve, real-time detection becomes more important for protecting businesses and customers.

Defending applications from fraud and abuse requires continuously advancing threat detection beyond traditional, point-in-time checks. To do that, modern security systems must address two compounding challenges simultaneously:.

According to recent reports, fraud and abuse operate as networks: Bad actors hide behind residential proxies and synthetic identities to create deceptive ad campaigns. Each of the attributes like location proxies, account, and identity parameters  appear benign in isolation. But behind the scenes, bad actors share payment methods, domains, and accounts, requiring security systems to target entire coordinated clusters of fraud rather than isolated indicators. This is hard to capture with traditional approaches that do not understand the relationship between attributes and evaluates each signal separately.

According to recent reports, detection must scale dynamically: As the graph-based abuse detection platform grew, the previous system, based on offline MapReduce batch processing, became bottlenecked. Tracing multi-hop relationships in batch MapReduce required repeated, expensive joins across distributed stages, triggering massive intermediate data expansions, heavy shuffle overhead, and network bottlenecks that caused hours-long latencies and combinatorial fanouts during multi-hop traversals.

In a recent development, in critical scenarios like halting live malware campaigns, multi-hour latency gaps leave room for a lot of damage. To block sophisticated fraud rings, Google needed to evaluate multi-hop relationship risks in real time at the time of serving these ads, before malicious content reaches users.

In a recent development, to overcome the limits of processing at inference time, the engineering team needed a database that could ingest live signals from a large number of sources via pub/sub streams, all while delivering horizontal elasticity, global transactional consistency, and sub-second multi-hop traversals. The solution was to modernize Google's graph-based abuse detection platform for Ads onto Spanner Graph.

Because Ads’ core transactional and entity data already lived in Spanner, they didn’t need to migrate any data in order to adopt Spanner Graph. Rather than standing up a separate, specialized graph database, the team simply defined property graphs directly on top of their existing relational tables.

This delivered several benefits:.

Industry observers note that from hour-long batch jobs to sub-second queries: Spanner Graph co-locates graph traversal computations directly with the underlying distributed data splits to minimize join overhead. Multi-hop traversals that previously took an hour in offline Apache Flume MapReduce jobs now execute on live production data with sub-second to single-digit millisecond latency.

Recent findings suggest that zero-ETL adoption in weeks, not months: Because there was no data to move, most graph-based abuse detection use cases transitioned to Spanner Graph within weeks. Layering a graph directly onto existing Spanner tables eliminated fragile synchronization pipelines and redundant storage costs.

Expressive pattern matching with native ISO GQL: Instead of writing and maintaining complex custom traversal code, engineers now query the exact same tables using standard ISO Graph Query Language (GQL), significantly accelerating feature velocity.

In a recent development, with Spanner Graph, Google's graph-based abuse detection platform for ads performs multi-hop pattern matching directly against operational relational data using ISO GQL. For instance, when an account is flagged for suspicious activity, the platform does real-time traversals to uncover all connected signals across the graph. This allows security systems to identify and disable entire coordinated fraud rings quickly rather than handling individual accounts sequentially.

Today, the graph-based abuse detection platform operates as a unified, Google-wide defense platform across a live graph of over 500 billion nodes and 1 trillion edges. Further, bringing ability to do multi-hop graph queries to real-time enforcement has fundamentally changed how Google stops abuse, delivering big wins for customers and end customers:.

Sources indicate that safeguarding advertiser budgets: The graph-based abuse detection platform is a primary source of detection signals for ad policy enforcement across Google's ad products. By uncovering the coordinated networks behind click fraud, click farms, and invalid traffic in real time, it stops bad actors, so advertisers don’t waste budget on invalid interactions.

Defending users against emerging threats: Real-time relationship analysis helps Google catch public-figure impersonation, account takeovers, cloaking, and landing-page malware before campaigns start to scale. During any incident, the graph-based abuse detection platform plays a vital role in tracing the connected assets and rapidly shutting down the attack.

Stopping repeat financial offenders: By correlating billing, financial, and identity information the platform identifies repeat bad actors and prevents banned offenders from simply spinning up new accounts to evade enforcement.

According to recent reports, google's graph-based abuse detection platform for ads shows what Spanner Graph can deliver under the world’s most demanding scale and latency requirements. Because this unified relational and graph architecture is built directly into Spanner, enterprises across a variety of industries can use the same foundation to solve their own complex pattern-matching and fraud challenges:.

Recent findings suggest that retail and e-commerce: Retailers connect customer accounts, payments, and shipping data to stop promo abuse and bot networks at checkout. For instance, Target rebuilt its Gift Finder using Spanner Graph and vector search (GraphRAG), cutting maintenance by 50% with sub-10ms latency. Additionally, PayPal uses Spanner Graph for its Customer Graph to unify customer identities across brands.

Sources indicate that cybersecurity and threat intelligence: Security teams map network assets, login origins, and access permissions to uncover attack paths and isolate compromised infrastructure during live incidents. Unifying graph queries with relational telemetry in Spanner helps expose proxy networks and automated impersonators before lateral movement occurs.

Financial services and payments: Risk teams correlate billing data and payment instruments to stop synthetic identity rings and fraud. Equifax uses Spanner Graph to map ownership hierarchies across 30 million businesses.

Introducing Falcon ASR

📅 07 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1271 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%.
  • We’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect.
  • In our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%.

We’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect. Developed at the Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in Abu Dhabi, it also supports English, French, Spanish and Portuguese.

In our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used. On our internal Emirati evaluation, it recorded the lowest word and character error rates among the systems we compared.

We also support word-level timestamps for transcriptions, linking each transcribed word to its position in the audio.

Arabic speech varies by region, speaker and setting. A model that handles a formal news broadcast may still struggle with a conversation in Emirati or with speech recorded over a phone line. Dialectal Arabic also has fewer transcribed resources than Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), which makes training and evaluation harder.

In a recent development, we trained Falcon-ASR on Emirati, MSA, other Gulf and Arabic dialects, and English. Our aim is to transcribe the words people use in everyday speech, including dialectal forms and changes between languages.

Recent findings suggest that the Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard, maintained by the ELM Research Center, ranks systems by the equal-weight average WER across six test sets. It also reports character error rate (CER). Lower values are better for both metrics. Our Falcon-ASR evaluation follows this protocol.

Sources indicate that WER = Word Error Rate; CER = Character Error Rate. A lower value indicates better performance.

According to recent reports, we evaluated Falcon-ASR on the same six benchmarks using the leaderboard’s pinned manifests. Competitor figures are the published leaderboard averages checked on 30 September 2026. Falcon-ASR’s average WER is 2.25 percentage points better than the best published result in that snapshot.

It has been revealed that public evaluation data already includes Emirati: Casablanca has a UAE subset. We complement that coverage with an internal evaluation of additional Emirati and Gulf speech, using held-out recordings and human-validated transcripts to assess transcription accuracy beyond the public UAE subset.

In our internal Emirati evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved 22.73% WER and 10.19% CER:.

Industry observers note that falcon-ASR has the lowest WER and CER among the systems compared here. Its WER is 4.07 percentage points below Qwen3-Omni, the next best result. The results show improved transcription accuracy at both the word and character level on this evaluation.

Sources indicate that we included background noise, overlapping speech, music, room reverberation and telephony effects, as well as variations in speed and pitch. We applied the same treatment to Emirati recordings, exposing the model to a range of conditions it may encounter in meetings, calls and other everyday recordings.

According to recent reports, falcon-ASR also transcribes English with the same model weights. In our evaluation on the seven public English test sets used by the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard, it achieved a mean WER of 5.74%.

The model also supports French, Spanish and Portuguese. All five languages use the same weights, without requiring a language flag. The output is a transcript in the language spoken.

According to recent reports, falcon-ASR builds on our Falcon3-Audio work. The architecture and training approach for Falcon3-Audio are described in Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data.

Our Hugging Face Demo Space lets you try Falcon-ASR and explore its transcription capabilities. API access and native applications are planned. We invite you to try the Demo with your own recordings.

We thank the team behind the Falcon-Emirati model for their support with Arabic foundation models. Read about their latest work in the Falcon-Emirati blog post.

We also extend our sincere thanks to Mikhail Lubinets for continued support with the compute infrastructure.

Industry observers note that نقدّم Falcon-ASR، نموذجنا للتعرف على الكلام العربي بحجم 1.6 مليار معلمة، مع اهتمام خاص باللهجة الإماراتية. طوّرنا النموذج في معهد الابتكار التكنولوجي (TII) في أبوظبي، وهو يدعم أيضًا اللغات الإنجليزية والفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية.

It has been revealed that في تقييمنا، حقق Falcon-ASR متوسط معدل خطأ في الكلمات بلغ 20.92% عبر ست مجموعات اختبار باللغة العربية، مقارنةً بأفضل نتيجة منشورة بلغت 23.17% في نسخة لوحة المتصدرين التي استخدمناها. وفي تقييمنا الداخلي للهجة الإماراتية، سجّل النموذج أدنى معدلات خطأ في الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة التي قارناها.

ندعم أيضاً الطوابع الزمنية على مستوى الكلمات في عمليات التفريغ النصي، بحيث ترتبط كل كلمة بموضعها في التسجيل الصوتي.

Sources indicate that يختلف الكلام العربي باختلاف المنطقة والمتحدث وظروف التسجيل. فقد ينجح نموذج في تفريغ نشرة إخبارية رسمية، ثم يجد صعوبة في تفريغ محادثة باللهجة الإماراتية أو تسجيل عبر الهاتف. كما أن الموارد الصوتية المفرّغة نصيًا للهجات العربية أقل من تلك المتاحة للعربية الفصحى، مما يزيد صعوبة التدريب والتقييم.

درّبنا Falcon-ASR على اللهجة الإماراتية والعربية الفصحى ولهجات خليجية وعربية أخرى، إلى جانب الإنجليزية. وهدفنا هو تفريغ الكلمات التي يستخدمها الناس في حديثهم اليومي، بما في ذلك الصيغ اللهجية والانتقال بين اللغات.

In a recent development, ترتّب لوحة المتصدرين المفتوحة الشاملة للتعرف على الكلام العربي، التي يديرها مركز ELM للأبحاث، الأنظمة وفق متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات عبر ست مجموعات اختبار، بوزن متساوٍ لكل مجموعة. وتعرض أيضًا معدل خطأ الأحرف (CER). وكلما انخفضت قيمة أي من المقياسين، كان الأداء أفضل. ويتبع تقييمنا للنموذج هذا البروتوكول.

WER هو معدل خطأ الكلمات؛ وCER هو معدل خطأ الأحرف. تشير القيمة الأقل إلى أداء أفضل.

قيّمنا Falcon-ASR على مجموعات الاختبار الست نفسها، باستخدام قوائم العينات المثبّتة في لوحة المتصدرين. وأرقام النماذج المنافسة هي المتوسطات المنشورة في اللوحة، والتي جرى التحقق منها في 30 سبتمبر 2026. وكان متوسط خطأ الكلمات للنموذج أفضل بمقدار 2.25 نقطة مئوية من أفضل نتيجة منشورة في تلك النسخة.

It has been revealed that تتوافر بالفعل بيانات عامة لتقييم اللهجة الإماراتية، إذ تضم مجموعة Casablanca قسمًا خاصًا بالإمارات. ونكمّل هذه التغطية بتقييم داخلي لتسجيلات إضافية من الكلام الإماراتي والخليجي، باستخدام تسجيلات مخصّصة للاختبار ونصوص مرجعية خضعت لمراجعة بشرية، لتقييم دقة التفريغ على مواد إضافية إلى جانب البيانات الإماراتية العامة.

حقق Falcon-ASR في تقييمنا الإماراتي الداخلي معدل خطأ كلمات قدره 22.73٪ ومعدل خطأ أحرف قدره 10.19٪:.

According to recent reports, سجّل Falcon-ASR أقل معدل لخطأ الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة المقارَنة هنا. وكان معدل خطأ الكلمات أقل بمقدار 4.07 نقطة مئوية من Qwen3-Omni، صاحب النتيجة التالية. وتُظهر النتائج تحسنًا في دقة التفريغ على مستوى الكلمات والأحرف في هذا التقييم.

Industry observers note that ضمّنا بيانات التدريب ضوضاء خلفية وكلامًا متداخلًا وموسيقى وصدى الصوت وتأثيرات الاتصالات الهاتفية، إلى جانب تغيّرات في سرعة الكلام وحدّة الصوت. وطبّقنا المعالجة نفسها على التسجيلات الإماراتية، لتهيئة النموذج للتعامل مع ظروف مختلفة قد يواجهها في الاجتماعات والمكالمات والتسجيلات اليومية الأخرى.

يفرّغ Falcon-ASR الكلام الإنجليزي باستخدام أوزان النموذج نفسها. وفي تقييمنا على مجموعات الاختبار الإنجليزية العامة السبع المستخدمة في لوحة Hugging Face المفتوحة للتعرف على الكلام، بلغ متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات 5.74٪.

يدعم النموذج أيضًا الفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية. وتستخدم اللغات الخمس أوزانًا واحدة، دون الحاجة إلى تحديد اللغة مسبقًا. ويكون الناتج تفريغًا نصيًا باللغة المنطوقة.

يستند Falcon-ASR إلى أعمالنا في Falcon3-Audio. وتعرض ورقة Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data بنية Falcon3-Audio ونهج تدريبه.

It has been revealed that يتيح عرضنا التجريبي على Hugging Face تجربة Falcon-ASR واستكشاف قدراته في تفريغ الكلام. أما الوصول عبر واجهة API والتطبيقات الأصلية فهو مخطّط له. ندعوكم إلى تجربة النموذج باستخدام تسجيلاتكم.

Sources indicate that نتوجّه بجزيل الشكر إلى الفريق القائم على تطوير نموذج Falcon-Emirati على دعمهم في مجال النماذج التأسيسية للغة العربية. ويمكن الاطّلاع على أحدث أعمال الفريق من خلال المقال المنشور حول Falcon-Emirati.

كما نتقدّم بخالص الشكر والتقدير إلى Mikhail Lubinets على دعمه المستمر للبنية التحتية الحاسوبية.

Sources indicate that يعكيكم العافية علي المجهود الطيب... بس بغينا نشوف موديلات صوتية STSو TTS بالللهجة الإماراتية لو أمكن.

Industry News: Not All Interpretation Methods Are Created Equal: Tiered Evaluation of AI Interpretability

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (222 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.31833v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As AI transitions to sociotechnical deployments, uninterpretable models pose serious threats to reliability, public trust and contestability. However, not all interpretation methods are created equal: for interpretability to enhance deployment safety and effectiveness, interpretation methods must be evaluated in a tiered system to differentiate evidence levels of trustworthiness, rather than validated through isolated interpretation instances. Our core vision is that elevating the evaluation of interpretation methods to a core AI assessment metric will drive robust knowledge discovery from data (KDD) and ensure safe, contestable sociotechnical deployments of AI. To this end, we propose TRUST, a tiered evaluation framework that builds upon the Predictability-Computability-Stability (PCS) principles for Veridical Data Science (VDS) and the Predictive, Descriptive and Relevant (PDR) foundations. To differentiate interpretation methods effectively and systematically, TRUST grades interpretation across five tiers: Task-Aligned PDR Foundations, Rigorous Epistemic Grounding, Unifying Semantic Understanding, Scope Transferability, and Targeted Prospective Validation. We present a start-to-finish case study of the iterative Random Forest (iRF) family under TRUST and contrast it with other LLM interpretation methods that struggle to clear specific tiers. Finally, we conclude with brief initial thoughts on how TRUST principles can extend in autonomous agentic frameworks. Ultimately, the TRUST framework fosters contestability and epistemic grounding as foundational evaluation principles for human-machine workflows and, eventually, autonomous agentic workflows.

Tech Report: Perplexity and Intelligence

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1597 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that from afar, it might seem like modern AI is built similarly to how software has been built in previous decades: with a diverse set of techniques targeting specific capabilities.
  • I believe tracking the pace of progress on training better compressors is key to understanding the arc of advances in AI.
  • A simplified, but fundamentally informative, view of AI development is that first, one builds a large computer, then uses it to pretrain a model (compressor) on a large unstructured dataset, then applies a variety of techniques—like prompting, finetuning or reinforcement learning—in different contexts to elicit the latent capabilities of that model.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Jakub Pachocki, Chief Scientist at OpenAI.

Industry observers note that from afar, it might seem like modern AI is built similarly to how software has been built in previous decades: with a diverse set of techniques targeting specific capabilities. There are indeed a variety of methods, but rather than designing something from scratch, they are mostly harnessing the intelligence coming from a much simpler and less interpretable process: training a compressor (or, equivalently⁠(opens in a latest window), predictor) on a very large corpus of data.1.

I believe tracking the pace of progress on training better compressors is key to understanding the arc of advances in AI. In this post, I argue for establishing perplexity (or, equivalently, cross-entropy loss) as a metric to compare between model developers and inform shared safety standards. As a first step, I provide more transparency into pretraining progress at OpenAI. Publishing our internal perplexity measurements took some consideration; it gives competitors a clearer picture of where we stand, but that concern is outweighed by the urgency of establishing shared⁠(opens in a new window) safety measures across the industry. We at OpenAI hope for this to be a step towards building a shared scientific basis for future pacing efforts.

A simplified, but fundamentally informative, view of AI development is that first, one builds a large computer, then uses it to pretrain a model (compressor) on a large unstructured dataset, then applies a variety of techniques—like prompting, finetuning or reinforcement learning—in different contexts to elicit the latent capabilities of that model. Algorithmic progress can blur the distinction between training phases, but we can still separate the creation of the AI with hard-to-predict emergent capabilities (which I earlier dubbed “an alien mind⁠”) and the subsequent targeted elicitation.

The primary way we measure progress on this key “intelligence substrate” has remained remarkably constant over the years—we have been tracking the perplexity of the models on a held-out dataset.2, 3 Perplexity measures how well a model predicts the next token on average; lower perplexity means better predictions. The plot opening this blog post indicates how this metric evolved for our models starting with GPT‑3.5.

The range of capabilities of models that are largely described by this one metric is stunning. Setting the fresh perplexity state-of-the-art on older datasets4, GPT‑2 was arguably the first model capable of consistently formulating coherent paragraphs of text. The next major leap, GPT‑3, was capable of learning in context, given a few examples of a task. GPT‑3.5, at a log-perplexity of ~0.99 on our current main evaluation dataset, was capable of fluent conversation and formed the basis for the original ChatGPT. GPT‑4, at ~0.91, was proficient at utilizing chain-of-thought reasoning productively, which motivated the subsequent targeted elicitation of this capability and the creation of modern reasoning models. Now, as we have reached losses below 0.8, we have seen the emergence of transformative capabilities in fields like cybersecurity and mathematics. I want to reemphasize that it was not at all clear a priori that these capabilities would appear once those precise perplexity thresholds are met—they can fundamentally be seen as emergent latent capabilities from progress on this one metric.

According to recent reports, as AI advances very rapidly, the scope and way in which we measure downstream capabilities may change quickly. It would make little sense to evaluate GPT‑2 and GPT‑3 on most modern benchmarks; and the benchmarks used then were largely saturated around GPT‑4. In contrast, I believe looking at progress on pretraining is likely to stay informative.

Sources indicate that A particular change in the pace of progress comes from the increasing contribution of AI to its own development. The most commonly discussed metrics revolve around AI augmenting and replacing human researchers in all stages of the development cycle; with an ultimate inflection point seen at “full recursive self-improvement”, where the process would be entirely automated with no human oversight. Apart from considering such a state as something we should obviously avoid for the sake of maintaining human control, I find this general framing misses something crucial. There is a potential step change that may come from AI participation in one key part of the development process: algorithmic research on pretraining.

In a recent development, we have recently witnessed unprecedented acceleration in another domain. For more than a year, we have been posing open problems in mathematics to our models as one of the ways of evaluating them. Once we upgraded to a model of log-perplexity ~0.76, it started producing groundbreaking results. For many of us that have previously worked in mathematics and adjacent fields, seeing the resolutions to questions we’ve long thought about coming out of the model one after another in a single Slack thread felt deeply surreal. Having experienced that allows us to extrapolate—such a sudden transformation is plausible in deep learning research too. While this field relies more on experimentation, there is a long history of simple insights being missed for years; and so as soon as 2027 we could conceivably see a similar avalanche of fundamental pretraining advancements5. While I expect AI will also significantly contribute to progress on alignment and monitoring, I think that progress is unlikely to be fast enough to allow the full potential acceleration in pretraining.

Industry observers note that given that the main way new surprising capabilities emerge is by progress on compression, a measure rooted in perplexity could give us a shared benchmark for general intelligence, regardless of the degree of automation of the development process. Extrapolating from recent progress, we should expect further transformative capabilities as we enter the ~0.68-0.7 log-perplexity window. I don’t know what those capabilities will be, and we may not be testing for them today. At the same time, we should also expect further degradation⁠(opens in a new window) in right now dominant forms of alignment auditing and further increases in evaluation and training awareness. I believe frontier model developers should jointly endeavour to establish shared norms for how to evaluate such models and red-team safety cases for them by the time they are first used, including shared transparency standards. I further propose common limits, based on perplexity and other measurements, that developers are committed to not crossing until our ability to understand and monitor AI behavior achieves a certain concrete milestone (such as the development of a successor to CoT monitors). That is, I’d like an industry standard that specifies a first limit on development, measured by some key metric we can track across labs, and what concretely we’d need to achieve before going beyond it. I hope that this leads the way to a common framework for setting successive limits and pacing further development.

Perplexity as a shared metric has challenges:.

Difficulty of comparison across labs. Different developers use different evaluation datasets and train on different data mixtures. Here, we report the numbers on the main dataset we have been tracking; I believe if we establish a goal of transparency we can find transferable ways to compare the quality of different base models.

In a recent development, detachment from actionable evaluations. Perplexity does not directly correspond to a task we care about. The reason to care about it is that we can expect advances on it to lead to emergence of entirely newly introduced capabilities.

Industry observers note that not accounting for advances outside of pretraining. Most notably, chain-of-thought reasoning does not reduce perplexity achieved by the model, even though it leads to a drastic increase in capabilities.

Unknown floor. We do not expect it is possible to achieve a loss of 0, which would correspond to being able to predict the dataset entirely deterministically. But we do not know what the inherent entropy of the data is. As we approach it, the apparent progress on perplexity will slow, but smaller gains on perplexity will correspond to larger leaps in model intelligence.

Sources indicate that at the same time, perplexity has stood the test of time as a metric many research teams have put a lot of effort into optimizing, and it continues to deliver consistent gains on general intelligence. I believe it can play an important role in standardizing how we talk about AI progress, and hope to see more transparency about it across the industry.

It’s vital to note that “compressor” in this sense is something that is capable of performing compression by predicting unseen data, not a compressed artifact like a GZIP file - that is, the best compressor trained on a given corpus does not necessarily “remember” the contents of the corpus.

In practice, we generally track the log of perplexity, also called cross-entropy loss.

The primary held-out datasets we’ve been using since GPT-3.5 are sourced from our internal codebase, and those are the numbers reported here (for a fixed snapshot).

Given what GPT‑2 and GPT‑3 were trained on, how well they predict code is a poor proxy for their general capabilities. This showcases a potential challenge arising from dataset selection with using perplexity as a shared metric; however it should still be informative to evaluate them jointly with modern models on general text. I chose to report perplexity on our internal codebase because I wanted to share the numbers we rely on most today to gauge progress in pretraining at OpenAI.

On the plot of losses of OpenAI models, you can see a steep acceleration in 2026. We attribute it mostly to the outcomes of long term research and compute investments, and only in a smaller part to automation. However, for the most recent models, we have already seen meaningful design contributions coming from AI⁠.

The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself

📅 08 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1554 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1.
  • Over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way.
  • Recent findings suggest that the first message is where I spend my effort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1. The official one is a 9B model that needs about 20 GB of memory and thinks for thousands of tokens before writing a single paragraph. On the Hub, I found only compressed copies of that same 9B model. So I described what I wanted to ML Intern, and the next day I had a 0.8B version that runs on a CPU. It returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens. The compute for the whole project, including having the 9B model label 8,797 example requests, came to USD 16.

Over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way. Each one started as a message in HuggingChat with ML-intern switched on, and each one ended as a public model on the Hub with its evaluation in the model card. ML-intern prepares the work, asks me for a budget before it spends anything, runs a small test before the real job, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware.

Recent findings suggest that the first message is where I spend my effort. My first prompt, for the citrus model shared below, was about 450 words. By my 6th project it was closer to 2,000, because each project taught me something I wanted in the next one. All seven prompts are on GitHub at yvrjsharma/ml-intern-prompts, exactly as I wrote them.

Recent findings suggest that A prompt starts with the idea in one line and why I want it. Then it names the exact pieces: the dataset, the base model, the training script. Anything I have already checked goes under a heading that literally says "Verified facts, do not re-derive", so the agent spends its budget on the work instead of rediscovering what I know. For the camera-angle LoRA that section listed which trainer had just added transparent-image support, and which open GitHub issues made the fallback trainer risky.

Two lines in the prompt are critical. The first asks for a baseline before any training. For example, the citrus prompt claims: "Also report the base model's zero-shot score on the same metric before training so we can see the gain." Without it you get a trained model and no idea whether it is better than what you started with. The second is a smoke test with a check attached. For the image LoRAs I asked for 50 training steps, then a check that the saved weights had actually changed, before paying for the full run.

It has been revealed that at the end of the prompt, I lay out the expected deliverables and limit the cost. I define what belongs in the model card and include a instruction like: "Cap total spend at USD 12 and ask me before exceeding it." Because ML-intern begins every task with zero dollar budget and needs permission before executing paid jobs, this spending limit stays strictly enforced. When you leave out a budget, the agent suggests a couple of paths depending on project size and asks which one you prefer.

Recent findings suggest that you don't necessarily need all of that on your first attempt. For example, I didn't have the verified-facts section in my citrus brief and ML Intern still produced a model that more than tripled the accuracy of the Qwen3.5-2B model. Let me walk you through 6 things I built with Ml-Intern in just a couple of days.

Industry observers note that A general vision model can describe a yellowing citrus leaf. However, telling you whether it is a mite problem or a magnesium deficiency, and the bio and non-bio remedies to treat the plant is very hard. Using Claude, I put together a training dataset merged from three sources hosted by the Project-AgML organization on the Hub. The resulting citrus-disease-vlm-instruct is a dataset containing 3,017 annotated images across 21 distinct pests, illnesses, nutritional gaps, and treatment approaches. ML-intern handled the fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-2B using these examples, making sure to benchmark the foundation model beforehand.

On the 335 test photos, the base model named the right problem 14.9% of the time. After two epochs on one A10G, the fine-tuned model got 52.8%. Compute cost, about USD 1.90.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Citrus Doctor App.

In a recent development, image models know plenty of characters. Huggy, drawn in the flat style of the Hugging Face brand assets, was not one of them. I asked ML-Intern for a LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B, trained on 84 captioned drawings from Chunte/huggy_for_training dataset.

In a recent development, the agent saved a checkpoint every 100 steps and drew the same set of prompts with each one, which made choosing easy. Step 200 was the first where Huggy was fully on-model. From step 500 on, Huggy's style started bleeding into prompts that had nothing to do with Huggy! The trained LoRA also works on the distilled klein model at 4 steps. Compute cost, about USD 7.60.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Huggy Generator App.

According to recent reports, ML-intern rendered 1,030 scanned household objects from Google Scanned Objects at 24 angles each, 24,722 transparent images, on a CPU job that cost a few cents. It later finalised 461 objects for training and 40 held out for testing, and 1,844 before-and-after training pairs spread evenly over 23 camera instructions.

Industry observers note that training ran 2,000 steps in about 90 minutes on one A100 (~USD 3.75). The whole project took about half a day and 48 jobs, counting the ones that failed on missing packages or wrong paths and had to be resubmitted by ML-Intern. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Viewpoint Orbit App.

No dataset existed for this, so my prompt described how to make one. Start from a real photo in Open Images, remove one object with the LaMa inpainting model, and draw a scribble where the object used to be. The untouched photo is the target. ML-intern wrote and tested the pair-building scripts in a CPU sandbox, then ran them as GPU jobs, recording the author and license of every source photo along the way. It built 6,042 training pairs and a 160-pair test set, where 40 of the test pairs come from 23 object classes kept out of training entirely.

Before training, it measured the base model on its own and with the Viggle turbo LoRA, and checked that running edits in batches produced identical images, which made the evaluation cheaper. Training ran 2,000 steps in 1 hour 38 minutes on one A100 (~USD 4), and a comparison of the saved checkpoints on 48 test pairs picked step 500.

Recent findings suggest that paired with the Viggle turbo LoRA at 6 steps the LoRA performed really well. 67.5% of objects detected where they were drawn, at 4.7 seconds per edit. Objects from the 23 unseen classes landed as reliably as the rest (65.0% versus 64.2%). The project took a little over a day and 59 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 24.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Doodle-in App.

Training the 0.8B and 2B students took 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G (USD 0.75 for both). The 0.8B also ships as an 812 MB GGUF file for running on a CPU. The project took about 11 hours and 24 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Pocket rewriter 0.8B Student · 2B Student · Dataset · Pocket Studio App · Compare the teacher-student in Rewriter Arena.

It took two runs. The first cached 155,000 training images as latents, baked the guidance into the model, then cut the step count in stages from 16 to 8 to 4, all on A100s. The 4-step student beat the teacher run at the same 4 steps on GenEval and FID, after that ML-intern exported it to ONNX for the browser. This run took about 13 hours and USD 22.

Recent findings suggest that I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. Total compute cost across both runs, about USD 37.

Check out: Agate 4-step model · Dataset · Run Agate in your browser · Agate 4-step LIVE.

These are the GPU and CPU job charges reported for each session.

ML-intern is in HuggingChat. Switch on ML-intern mode and paste a prompt. If you want a starting point, my example prompts are free to copy. Start from a model you wish existed and a dataset you have, or one you can describe. Give it a small budget, ask for a baseline and a smoke test, and read what comes back before you raise the cap.

According to recent reports, if you make something with it, share it on X and tag @Gradio and @HuggingFace. We would love to see the models you make that nobody else would think to build for you.

GaokaoMathGen: Chinese Gaokao Mathematics Finale Problem Generation Controlled by Latent Reasoning Structures

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (175 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.31823v2 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Generating Chinese Gaokao mathematics finale problems requires controlling not only the included skills, but also the underlying mathematical kernel and solution path. Existing LLM-based methods mainly rely on surface-level specifications, while the realized difficulty of generated problems cannot be determined directly from prompted targets. Therefore, we propose GaokaoMathGen, a framework for Chinese Gaokao mathematics finale problem generation controlled by latent reasoning structures. It extracts standardized latent reasoning structures from seed problems and performs constrained synthesis using skills, methods, a core identity, and a pivot step as structural controls. We further estimate realized difficulty through logical-quality filtering, fixed-solver decoding effort, structural features, and solver-output search signals. Experiments show that semantic normalization improves cross-annotator comparability and that 78.0% of 609 scored candidates pass the logical-quality filter. In a teacher audit of the 60 highest-effort candidates, all were judged to reach finale or penultimate problem difficulty, and only one exhibited a severe logical issue. These results support latent reasoning structures as effective control signals for generating high-difficulty mathematical problems.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon Cognito multi-Region replication (MRR) now supports additional AWS Regions, extending the resilience benefits of MRR to more workloads.
  • According to recent reports, previously, MRR was available in 16 commercial Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.
  • MRR is available as an add-on for user pools on the Essentials or Plus feature plans, and requires a multi-Region AWS KMS customer managed key (CMK).

Amazon Cognito multi-Region replication (MRR) now supports additional AWS Regions, extending the resilience benefits of MRR to more workloads. Amazon Cognito helps you implement secure sign-in and access control for users, AI agents, and microservices in minutes, and MRR lets you synchronize user and machine identity data, including credentials, user pool configurations, and federation setups, to a secondary user pool in a standby Region you designate in near real-time. With user data in the standby Region, you can redirect traffic and keep authentication available if there is a disruption in your primary Region.

According to recent reports, previously, MRR was available in 16 commercial Regions and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions. You can now also use MRR to replicate your user data to Asia Pacific (Hyderabad, Hong Kong, Jakarta, Malaysia, Melbourne, New Zealand, Osaka, Taipei, Thailand), Canada West (Calgary), Europe (Milan, Spain, Zurich), Israel (Tel Aviv), Mexico (Central), Africa (Cape Town) Regions, helping you meet resilience, data residency, and compliance requirements in the Regions that best align with your needs.

MRR is available as an add-on for user pools on the Essentials or Plus feature plans, and requires a multi-Region AWS KMS customer managed key (CMK). For the full list of AWS Regions where Amazon Cognito is available, see AWS Capabilities by Region. To get started, visit the developer guide for instructions and the pricing page for pricing details.

Tech Report: What’s fresh in Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1782 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, as organizations move from reactive analytics to proactive systems of action powered by autonomous AI agents, data platforms face a new set of demands.
  • In the Agentic Data Cloud, Apache Spark doesn't operate in isolation.
  • Today, we are announcing the general availability of Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0, debuting a next-generation runtime foundation for serverless and managed cluster deployments.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

In a recent development, as organizations move from reactive analytics to proactive systems of action powered by autonomous AI agents, data platforms face a new set of demands. Moving from human scale to agent scale changes both how data pipelines run and how they are built: Teams and AI agents now use Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools and agentic troubleshooting to build, submit, and diagnose Apache Spark pipelines while preparing multimodal datasets, performing feature engineering, and acting on live business signals around the clock. Over the past year, customer use of Managed Service for Apache Spark in serverless deployments has nearly doubled, with millions of jobs running each month as enterprises build on Google’s Agentic Data Cloud.

In the Agentic Data Cloud, Apache Spark doesn't operate in isolation. Managed Service for Apache Spark runs on Google Cloud's borderless lakehouse, so Apache Spark and BigQuery can read and write the same tables with high performance. Through Knowledge Catalog, both engines share centralized governance, consistent policies, detailed lineage, and semantic discovery for AI agents.

Today, we are announcing the general availability of Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0, debuting a next-generation runtime foundation for serverless and managed cluster deployments. Engineered to power both modern enterprise data pipelines and fast-growing agentic workloads, Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0 introduces:.

A upcoming 4.0 runtime with Apache Spark 4.2: Standardized on Apache Spark 4.2, Java 25, Python 3.13 with Pixi, and Apache Iceberg 1.12, it is now available for both serverless and managed clusters.

A redesigned, code-first Google Cloud console and agentic troubleshooting: Onboard quickly with a upcoming Overview page featuring a samples gallery, Lakehouse public datasets, and one-click VS Code authoring in Cloud Shell, manage all serverless and cluster workloads from a unified Jobs view, and use an AI agent to automatically diagnose job failures.

Third-party IDE integration with the Data Agent Kit: Configure MCP servers, skills, and API access to build and run Apache Spark pipelines directly from VS Code, Claude Code, and Antigravity.

Faster startups and Lightning Engine acceleration: Run on default Gen4 infrastructure with faster startups at no additional cost, and accelerate workloads with Lightning Engine for up to 3.25x the price-performance over the leading high-speed Apache Spark alternative.

This fresh runtime packages Apache Spark 4.2 (including Spark Declarative Pipelines and Real-Time Mode), Java 25, Scala 2.13, Apache Iceberg 1.12, Delta Lake 4.4, and Python 3.13 with Pixi for faster dependency management.

Managed Spark serverless and cluster workloads now run on the same modern stack whether written by a data engineer or generated by data engineering and data science skills in Gemini, Claude, and other large language models (LLMs). Teams can standardize on one set of component versions and move PySpark, Scala, and Spark SQL workloads between serverless and managed clusters.

Data teams should spend their time writing Spark logic rather than configuring infrastructure, hunting for the right job, or digging through driver and executor logs when something fails. Version 4.0 ships alongside a redesigned, code-first Google Cloud console built to take that operational work off their plate.

The refreshed console streamlines every stage of the Apache Spark lifecycle:.

Frictionless onboarding and one-click authoring: A redesigned Overview page helps developers get started immediately with an integrated samples gallery, pre-loaded Lakehouse public datasets, guided demos, and one-click authoring in VS Code through Cloud Shell.

Optimized defaults and reusable runtime profiles: Out-of-the-box performance defaults simplify job submission and cluster creation. With reusable runtime profiles (in preview) for batch and interactive workloads, platform admins can capture governed hardware, network, and autoscaling baselines once so developers can simply select a profile and run code.

Unified job, session, and fleet management: Engineers can submit and monitor batch jobs, interactive serverless sessions, and managed clusters from a single unified listing, backed by streamlined fleet management and redesigned detail views that surface key performance metrics and logs in one place.

Agentic troubleshooting: When a job fails or slows down, an AI agent analyzes logs, metrics, and query plans within existing IAM permissions to identify the likely root cause and recommend a fix, helping engineers promptly return a failed job to a healthy state.

Image 1: Gemini Cloud Assist investigates a failed Apache Spark job, forms a hypothesis, and points to the likely root cause without leaving the job page.

Image 2: One Jobs page for every Apache Spark workload across serverless and managed clusters, with tier and runtime version at a glance.

Many data engineers and data scientists would rather never leave their editor. With the Data Agent Kit, they can build and run Apache Spark workloads from VS Code, Antigravity, Claude Code, and other agentic IDEs. Setup takes a few clicks: pick Apache Spark and the other services you use, and the kit configures Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, agent skills, and API access for each one. From there, AI agents can generate, tune, and test Apache Spark pipelines on Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0 without leaving the IDE.

Image 3: In VS Code, the Data Agent Kit sets up MCP servers, skills, and API access for Apache Spark and other services.

According to recent reports, as practitioners and AI agents trigger short-running, ephemeral jobs on demand to prepare data, perform feature engineering, and answer ad-hoc queries, low startup latency and predictable price-performance are essential to avoiding a cost spiral. In Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0, our performance-optimized serverless experience removes manual infrastructure tuning through three changes:.

Faster startups at no additional cost: On the serverless Premium tier, runtime and control-plane optimizations in version 4.0 deliver faster startup times than previous runtime versions across interactive sessions and short-running batch workloads at no additional cost.

Hardware acceleration by default: Fresh serverless 4.0 workloads run on the Premium tier by default, using Google Cloud's latest-generation Gen4 VM instances and Hyperdisk storage. Teams get our highest-efficiency compute and storage fleet without picking machine types or configuring disks, while aligning infrastructure tiering directly with workload urgency.

Software acceleration with Lightning Engine: Our native C++ vectorized execution engine, Lightning Engine, is available in the 4.0 runtime and delivers up to 3.25x the price-performance over the leading high-speed Apache Spark alternative, along with up to 4.9x faster performance compared to running open-source Apache Spark with zero code changes. Built on Apache Gluten and Velox with Google-specific optimizations, Lightning Engine compiles Apache Spark DataFrame, Dataset, and Spark SQL query plans into native SIMD instructions. For lakehouse storage, built-in intelligent caching accelerates file scan times on Apache Iceberg tables by up to 50%. Separately, for workloads querying BigQuery, Lightning Engine's native reader uses Apache Arrow streams to accelerate BigQuery reads by up to 40% compared to default BigQuery reads in Managed Service for Apache Spark. In the 4.0 runtime, Lightning Engine expands support to ARM processors, Ubuntu images, and native vectorized readers for Apache ORC and CSV alongside Apache Parquet, Apache Iceberg, and Delta Lake.

"We were facing not only processing challenges, we were facing management overhead across thousands of servers in our ecosystem, so we migrated to serverless Managed Service for Apache Spark. We moved from managing infrastructure to a no-ops infrastructure. Not only did it help us overcome maintenance and cluster management challenges, it helped us optimize our costs at scale to meet our business SLAs. Apache Spark is no longer just compute for us; it is a strategic business accelerator."—Saurabh Kumar, Senior Director of Data Engineering, Lowe's.

It has been revealed that when autonomous agents and production pipelines run around the clock, tying a workload to a single machine shape or zone can stall downstream decisions when regional demand spikes. Without dedicated reservations, cloud service providers may not always have available capacity during peak demand. We are introducing infrastructure fungibility for serverless deployments to improve resource availability for all customers:.

It has been revealed that serverless infrastructure fungibility and fallback: Serverless 4.0 workloads are no longer tied to one VM instance family, disk type, or zone. The platform selects from several latest-generation VM instance families and disk types across zones in the region. If the preferred infrastructure is constrained during a local demand peak, the service automatically chooses the best available infrastructure in the same region instead of failing the job. Once capacity returns, workloads go back to the default Gen4 VM instances and Hyperdisk infrastructure.

According to recent reports, data Compute Unit (DCU) quotas: Quotas for serverless deployments are now set in DCUs rather than per machine family. Because the platform selects the VM instance family, admins manage one unified DCU quota instead of separate CPU quotas for each machine type.

A borderless lakehouse breaks down walled gardens by connecting operational, analytical, and cross-cloud data in open formats without moving it. In Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0, Apache Iceberg ships directly in the runtime image, and every workload automatically has access to the serverless Lakehouse runtime catalog. Teams no longer have to configure a lakehouse metastore with Apache Spark or complete prerequisites such as setting up Google Cloud Storage (GCS) directories beforehand, so they can focus straight on writing business logic. Version 4.0 also eliminates the need for GCS staging buckets and uses end-user credentials by default.

Recent findings suggest that through the Lakehouse runtime catalog, Managed Service for Apache Spark, BigQuery, and AlloyDB can directly read and write the same Apache Iceberg tables on GCS without ETL pipelines or data copies. Everything registered in the Lakehouse runtime catalog automatically surfaces in Knowledge Catalog, which enriches metadata and business context so AI agents and Gemini can query and reason over tables curated with Apache Spark with high accuracy, governed access controls, and lower token costs.

To see how these capabilities come together across end-to-end architectures, read our Google Cloud Apache Spark in the Agentic Era whitepaper. The whitepaper walks through practical design patterns for multimodal data preparation, large-scale feature engineering, and connecting AI agents to governed Apache Iceberg tables through MCP tools and Knowledge Catalog.

Sources indicate that managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0 is available for serverless and managed cluster deployments across all Managed Service for Apache Spark regions. The fastest way to try version 4.0 is the Data Agent Kit: install it in VS Code, Claude Code, or Antigravity to build and run Apache Spark workloads on version 4.0 with AI agents right from your IDE. You can also start from the new Overview page in the Google Cloud console, which walks you from code to a running job.

To learn more, read the Managed Service for Apache Spark 4.0 documentation for serverless deployments and managed clusters, and try the hands-on Lightning Engine codelab.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:.

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

In a recent development, edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Install the latest version of transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0):.

Serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:.

Recent findings suggest that the port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080, vLLM uses 8000, SGLang uses 30000, and LM Studio uses 1234. See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples.

Both LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:.

We can't wait to see what you build.

Compressible Representations: Functional Spines in Deep Neural Networks

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (247 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.31817v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep networks embed inputs in high-dimensional representations, but how much of this capacity actually drives behavior? We introduce a framework for identifying, at each layer, the subspace of the representation that is functionally sensitive to the task. Using a matrix analogous to the Fisher information but defined over the hidden representation, we rank directions by their influence on downstream computation and project onto the most task-sensitive subspace. Across pretrained vision networks, representations are remarkably compressible: a small fraction of the task-sensitive subspace preserves most performance, often requiring far fewer dimensions than geometric alternatives. We find that this compressed representation is also more robust to adversarial attacks generated on the full network. We additionally show that this decomposition recovers functionally distinct subspaces within the same representation: on cue-conflict stimuli, shape-sensitive and texture-sensitive directions are largely non-overlapping, and ablating one selectively impairs the corresponding task while leaving the other intact. Task-sensitive subspaces also provide a principled foundation for continual learning: constraining gradient updates to lie orthogonal to the task-sensitive subspaces of prior tasks outperforms standard variance-based gradient projection methods. Finally, restricting representational comparisons to task-sensitive subspaces reveals that inter-model alignment is higher in task-sensitive directions than in task-insensitive directions at later layers, and that conditioning on different tasks over the same stimuli uncovers asymmetries that full-space similarity measures cannot detect. Together, these results establish that deep networks compute through a low-dimensional functional spine embedded within a much larger representational space.

Richpanel⁠(opens in a fresh window) solves that using OpenAI models to both set up the tools and procedures AI support agents need to act and handle customer conversations.

It has been revealed that “The intelligence is no longer the bottleneck. It’s everything around it.”.

Industry observers note that deploying a support agent often requires a forward-deployed engineer to connect the agent to a customer’s systems and define how it should work. Amit saw that many companies didn’t have engineers to spare and asked himself, “What if that forward-deployed engineer itself was an AI agent?”.

So Richpanel built it: an AI manager to handle agent setup. Customers began calling it Boss AI. It writes procedures and defines how Richpanel’s frontline support agent, copilot, and quality-assurance agent call the tools they need.

Richpanel uses GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.1 Sol for Boss AI, prioritizing accuracy when building the tools and procedures its other agents will follow.

According to recent reports, richpanel designs the frontline agent to handle hundreds of thousands of conversations, making the cost of each interaction an key part of model selection. It uses GPT‑6 Luna and other OpenAI models for that work. Amit claims Richpanel takes the same approach to its copilot and quality-assurance agents.

“What matters is a balance of cost and intelligence,” Amit says. Richpanel’s customers may already use low-cost outsourced support. Automating their operations has to make financial sense against that starting point.

In a recent development, amit credits OpenAI with making models available that can handle long context and longer tasks while remaining cost efficient. Richpanel can use deeper reasoning to prepare its support agents and more economical models to run the conversations that follow.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for Oracle now supports Replica First Patching, which reduces downtime during minor version upgrades.
  • Sources indicate that replica First Patching helps you keep mission-critical Oracle workloads current on minor versions with less disruption.
  • Industry observers note that we recommend that you connect your applications through the Primary Endpoint when you use Replica First Patching.

Recent findings suggest that amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS) for Oracle now supports Replica First Patching, which reduces downtime during minor version upgrades. Replica First Patching is available for Enterprise Edition DB instances. With Replica First Patching, you apply a minor version upgrade to a replica in the same AWS Region first while your primary DB instance continues to serve traffic, and then switch over to the replica when you're ready to complete the upgrade. If the replica is in read-only mode, you can validate the fresh minor engine version with your read traffic.

Sources indicate that replica First Patching helps you keep mission-critical Oracle workloads current on minor versions with less disruption. You choose when to switch over within the switchover window, for example during a low-traffic period. If you don't switch over within the window, Amazon RDS rolls back the replica to its original minor engine version. After the switchover, Amazon RDS completes the upgrade on the new primary DB instance. Amazon RDS then upgrades your other replicas, including your former primary DB instance, to the same minor engine version.

Industry observers note that we recommend that you connect your applications through the Primary Endpoint when you use Replica First Patching. The Primary Endpoint is a DNS name that resolves to the current primary DB instance, so your applications reach the latest primary DB instance after the switchover without connection string changes.

It has been revealed that replica First Patching is available at no additional charge in all commercial AWS Regions where Amazon RDS for Oracle is available. Standard pricing applies to the replica DB instance. To learn more, see Upgrading with Replica First Patching in the Amazon RDS User Guide.

A Generative AI Agent to Emulate Interactive Human-driven Vehicles for Automated Driving Testing in Urban Areas

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (236 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2611.31797v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Realistic modeling of human-driven vehicle (HDV) interactions is essential for automated driving safety testing in urban areas. Existing methods struggle to reproduce realistic safety-critical interactions involving high collision risk for the following reasons: they often assume full observability, overlooking interactions arising from occlusion. Driving styles are mainly characterized by vehicle maneuvers, limiting the diversity of safety-critical interaction behaviors. Moreover, learning signals from safety-critical interactions can be diluted by non-critical driving behaviors. To address these concerns, we propose a generative AI agent to emulate interactive HDVs. The agent incorporates field-of-view modeling to account for driver visibility under occlusion and characterizes the interaction process using five metrics spanning its initial, intermediate, and final stages. It automatically learns diverse interaction styles through a dynamic mixture-of-experts network. Through residual reinforcement learning, the agent further refines generated trajectories to match the real-world distributions of safety-critical interaction characteristics. Experiments on the INTERACTION dataset show that our method reduces Jensen--Shannon divergence (JSD) by 39.9\%--87.1\% across five interaction characteristics compared with a state-of-the-art baseline. Our method achieves greater improvements of up to 87.1\% in final-stage interaction metrics, suggesting that it can reduce error accumulation in long-horizon trajectory generation. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each proposed component, particularly highlighting the importance of residual refinement. Generalization experiments show that our method approaches the performance of full training on unseen intersections with only one epoch of fine-tuning.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something upcoming, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:.

You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):.

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:.

FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

Pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

Recent findings suggest that with several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:.

In a recent development, add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

In a recent development, boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

Recent findings suggest that for edits, each region says where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:.

Everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

Black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:.

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:.

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

According to recent reports, A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as .

See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:.

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call.

Recent findings suggest that let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:.

In a recent development, FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

So one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

The text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

In a recent development, this gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:.

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

According to recent reports, in stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

At the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

It has been revealed that every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

Each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

Sources indicate that in FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

The noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

The distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Industry observers note that attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:.

Recent findings suggest that text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

Industry observers note that at every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps reveals how the image takes shape:.

The fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are upcoming to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

It has been revealed that get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:.
