📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

In global maritime logistics, Marine Ports and Terminals play a significant role in the movement of container and cargo, within and beyond. Marine ports and terminals world-wide use a Terminal Operating System (TOS) which acts as the central nervous system managing port operations 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. A modern TOS looks, automates and orchestrates every physical and digital activities, resources and events across Order-to-Invoice processes of a marine terminal.

Developed by Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), DynaPORT is a field-proven next-generation Terminal Operating System that provides a single, integrated operating backbone for multimodal and multipurpose terminals. It orchestrates the complete order-to-invoice lifecycle across vessel, rail, truck, and barge operations, while supporting containers, general cargo, dry and liquid bulk, break-bulk, and roll-on/roll-off cargo. By automating end-to-end terminal workflows, DynaPORT delivers real-time operational visibility into operations while optimizing assets and resources to drive improvement of key business performance indicators.

One of India’s largest commercial port developers and operators has relied on DynaPORT for more than two decades across its cargo terminals, supporting the management of bulk, break-bulk, and liquid cargo. To modernize the platform’s architecture, TCS partnered with the customer to achieve a landmark milestone: migrating DynaPORT to a modern, cloud-based architecture.

Sources indicate that the Port Operator & TCS partnered with Google Cloud to execute an ambitious cloud modernization journey. Modeled after the architectural principles of high-velocity Google Cloud enterprise transformations—this case study details the systematic deconstruction of legacy technical debt, the strategic rationale and enterprise differentiators of choosing AlloyDB for PostgreSQL, the target Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) and AlloyDB cloud-native architecture, the heterogeneous migration of over 1.2 million lines of code using Google Cloud Database Migration Service (DMS).

According to recent reports, enterprise logistics platforms that evolve over decades inevitably accumulate architectural debt, particularly through tightly coupled components. DynaPORT Cargo followed this pattern: successive releases and architectural transitions gradually transformed the platform into a classic multi-tier monolith, with its components carrying significant technical debt.

Over years of optimization for sub-millisecond on-premises database round-trips, fundamental business logic had been progressively migrated out of the application tier and embedded directly into the database engine. In the DynaPORT Cargo module alone, the core schema contained:.

262 Packages containing over 1.2 million lines of code.

54 Stored Procedures, 53 Functions, and 63 Database Triggers.

Cross-schema User-Defined Types (UDTs).

Critical business operations—such as multi-tiered marine invoice tariff calculations, dynamic slab rating, berth allocation planning, yard truck assignments, and autonomous error logging—were entirely governed by complex, multi-thousand-line PL/SQL procedures. The database was no longer merely a relational persistence store; it was the primary execution engine of the enterprise.

The application tier was hosted on monolithic WebLogic and WildFly application servers running on static on-premises virtual machines. The application relied on legacy Java Enterprise features, including Enterprise JavaBeans (EJBs), custom Object-Relational Mapping (ORM) dialects, and heavy configuration state. Modules including Revenue Management, Berth Planning, Gate Operations, and Reporting shared common JVM heaps across application servers. A performance spike in batch invoice generation could starve memory from real-time Handheld Terminals (HHT) used by container crane operators on the quayside.

Because business logic was fragmented across Java application binaries and raw database packages, continuous delivery was practically non-existent:.

Manual Deployment Runbooks: Releases required multi-hour maintenance windows involving manual execution of sequential SQL scripts, package recompilations, and server restarts.

High Regression Risk: In the legacy schema with 262 interdependent packages, modifying a single package specification frequently invalidated dozens of dependent functions, views, and synonyms, triggering cascading runtime failures.

Environment Drift: Development, testing, and production environments suffered from configuration divergence, requiring lengthy manual reconciliation before any production cutover.

Licensing fees scaled linearly with physical CPU core counts, penalizing the business whenever hardware was scaled to accommodate peak cargo vessel traffic. Furthermore, high-availability setups required complex shared storage arrays, specialized interconnects, and heavy administrative overhead from dedicated database administrators (DBAs).

When architecting the cloud transformation, the joint architecture teams from the customer, TCS, and Google Cloud evaluated two fundamentally different modernization strategies:.

Strategy A: Database-Agnostic Migration.

Strategy B: Modernization using AlloyDB.

Extract all business logic from the database tier and rewrite it into Java application-tier services (HQL / Spring Data).

Retain optimized procedural logic in the database tier, converting to PostgreSQL PL/pgSQL on AlloyDB.

It has been revealed that massive. Complete rewrite of thousands of data access objects, ORM mappings, and transaction boundaries.

Sources indicate that moderate. Focused remediation of syntax, metadata, and database dialect differences; application remains stable.

Multiple person-years; prohibitive time-to-market.

Target delivery achievable in agile sprints; low operational disruption.

Network latency amplification due to multiple network hops for complex set operations previously run in-database.

Native in-engine execution with sub-millisecond response times, backed by AlloyDB’s accelerated storage and compute engine.

Rejected due to timeline risks and massive business disruption.

Selected as the winning enterprise target path.

The target cloud architecture was designed according to the Google Cloud Architecture Framework, transforming the monolithic JEE middleware into modern containerized microservices orchestrated on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), coupled with an enterprise AlloyDB for PostgreSQL cluster.

It has been revealed that the cornerstone of the migration was converting over 1.2 million lines of deeply intertwined Oracle PL/SQL procedural logic into PostgreSQL PL/pgSQL. The team utilized Google Cloud Database Migration Service (DMS) with its built-in Conversion Workspaces and Gemini-assisted AI code refactoring to accelerate bulk transformations.

While DMS automatically converted the majority of standard DDL constructs, functions, and queries, the remaining (~15%) involved complex Oracle proprietary idioms that required targeted engineering remediation. Couple of examples of the manual intervention.

Technical Pattern & Remediation.

Modernized AlloyDB PL/pgSQL Equivalent.

Architectural Remediation & Runtime Impact.

TYPE_L := array_append(TYPE_L, rec); or TYPE_L[cardinality(TYPE_L)+1] := rec;.

Replaced unsupported .EXTEND method on nested tables with native PostgreSQL array concatenation and dynamic index expansion.

SELECT ROWNUM FROM PTY_IM WHERE ROWNUM <= N;.

SELECT s.idx FROM generate_series(1, N) AS s(idx);.

Eliminated physical dummy table hacks (PTY_IM) in favor of in-memory, set-returning generator functions with zero disk I/O.

In April 2026, the modernized DynaPORT platform on Google Cloud went live in production at one of the newest ports in India, achieving a seamless, low downtime cutover. By Aug’26, 3 more terminals have gone live on this.

Modernized Google Cloud & AlloyDB Stack.

Variable query latency during batch spikes; table bloat requiring manual DBA reindexing.

Upto 2x transactional throughput, sub-second read query responses, automated ML vacuuming and memory optimization.

Complex SAN failover; multi-minute outages during planned database maintenance.

Sub-second automatic failover, 99.99% availability SLA inclusive of maintenance, zero transaction loss.

Multi-week release cycles; high-risk manual database patching; frequent regression problems.

Containerized rolling updates on GKE and non-blocking transactional DDL deployments in AlloyDB.

Punitive per-core enterprise licenses; high on-prem hardware and maintenance overhead.

About 50% reduction in database TCO; completely open-source compatible with transparent, predictable cloud pricing.

Rigid vertical hardware limits; slow hardware procurement cycles.

Instantaneous horizontal elasticity across GKE container pods and AlloyDB read pools.

The successful cloud migration of DynaPORT yields three fundamental architectural lessons for enterprise IT leaders:.

Industry observers note that do Not Throw Away Proven Intellectual Property: Fully rewriting mission-critical procedural logic into application code is often a high-risk anti-pattern. Migrating from Oracle PL/SQL to open PL/pgSQL on an accelerated engine like AlloyDB preserves decades of tested business rules while modernizing the infrastructure platform.

Select Database Engines Built for Cloud Realities: Standard open-source relational engines often struggle with extreme enterprise throughput without extensive tuning. AlloyDB’s disaggregated storage architecture, columnar acceleration, and built-in ML intelligence provide the enterprise muscle needed to replace legacy commercial database engines.

Containerize Application Workloads on GKE: Decoupling the application tier into independently scalable container pods on Google Kubernetes Engine provides the elasticity and resilience necessary to absorb rapid operational surges without affecting core database stability.

We will engage as an vital stakeholder to evaluate your current legacy setup and help design a low-risk, high-performance migration pathway using Google Cloud services like AlloyDB and Google Kubernetes Engine.

Constructive Causal Abstraction and a Case Study in Mechanistic Interpretability

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (225 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.31795v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: Existing frameworks in causal abstraction first propose a high-level causal model, and then verify whether its interventional effects agree with those of a given micro-level model - the two models are declared causally consistent when the discrepancy is zero. However, proposing a consistent macro causal model is difficult, because macro causal relations are almost never well-defined, since distinct micro-level interventions associated with the same apparent macro intervention can produce different effects. Our central insight is that causally consistent macro-level models can be obtained constructively: ill-defined macro interventions can be interpreted as missing variables on the macro level, and can be accounted for by introducing a complementary variable q that retains omitted causally relevant state. In the linear case, q has a unique form and we provide sufficient conditions for valid implementations to exist; in the nonlinear case, we provide an ODE-based algorithm for constructing implementations. We call this framework Constructive Causal Abstraction (CCA), and use CCA to formulate the difference between machine-learning model auditing and editing. With the Bias-in-Bios biographies dataset, we demonstrate that CCA allows practitioners to articulate assumptions when detecting the model's gender bias. Finally, CCA resolves a well-known paradox known as "interpretability illusion" which points to a mismatch between the subspace for editing and the one where the model implements a signal-to-output pathway.

Sources indicate that AWS Compute Optimizer automation rules can now target the organizational units (OUs) you manage with AWS Organizations, making it easier for large organizations to scale optimization across their accounts. Previously, management accounts could target up to 50 member accounts per rule. Now, a single rule can cover every account in an OU, including accounts added later. You also have the flexibility to exclude specific child OUs or member accounts as needed. Automation rules help you save cost and improve performance by applying recommended actions on a daily, weekly, or monthly schedule when they match your criteria. These actions include cleaning up unattached Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes and upgrading volumes to the latest-generation volume types. For example, from your management account, you can create an automation rule to clean up unattached volumes across your entire organization, while allowing resource owners to tag and exclude volumes they want to keep. To get started, turn on Automation for your selected OUs. Then, create rules that target them. Support for OUs is available in all AWS Regions where Compute Optimizer automation rules are available. To learn more, see Enabling Automation for your organization in the AWS Compute Optimizer User Guide, or visit the AWS Compute Optimizer product page.

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.31794v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Frontier models are increasingly used through harnesses as agents, with growing autonomy to do useful work. Agent performance can often be enhanced by the use of skills: reusable workflows, code, and prompts that provide task-related information or guide the behaviour of the model. Skills, being textual in nature, present themselves as another editable surface to be optimized; current methods have improved on handcrafting and one-shot generation by treating skill development as an iterative process, using score-driven search to tweak and improve performance. In this paper, we demonstrate the efficacy of the agents themselves as optimizers: across five benchmarks, a coding agent without guidance substantially improves every target and outperforms published skill-optimization methods. More broadly, this shows the capability of agents to do such work and to refine their own behaviour to provide task-specific context, as long as they are given a metric to measure against.

Breaking: Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta

📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3057 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta.
  • Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.
  • Sources indicate that meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input.

Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.

Sources indicate that meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post demonstrates you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here.

Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that looks, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images.

The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4.

Muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the upcoming modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each.

Recent findings suggest that the language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum.

Industry observers note that muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang recipes below.

Sources indicate that A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention.

Recent findings suggest that muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images.

According to recent reports, muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm.

In a recent development, the context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text.

Grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context.

According to recent reports, the Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template.

Use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed.

You can initialize the model and processor as follows.

It has been revealed that prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template, enabling add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=True, return_dict=True, and return_tensors="pt". Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt.

The Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt.

According to recent reports, video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor:.

As a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template.

Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate.

The Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference.

If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood:.

Sources indicate that the processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings.

It has been revealed that muse Spark Open can do text-only and multimodal tool calling. You can make the model call tools as follows.

Muse Spark Open uses a channel-based chat template (Harmony, first introduced by gpt-oss). Note that you don’t have to know about the internals, but it’s useful to check the channels the model routes to, in case you get low quality outputs. In the input message below:.

Muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit, ready to use right away.

It has been revealed that you can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer. This section demonstrates how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples.

First, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP and split the experts across GPUs, using DistributedConfig, which tells transformers how to split the model when it loads:.

According to recent reports, in the snippet above, fsdp_size=64 shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and ep_size=8 splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch.

Sources indicate that now, we can configure the SFTConfig for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case.

The core parts here are packing=True which joins examples into 2048-token sequences without padding. A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. save_only_model=True saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. LoraConfig targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen.

Then we can run this command across each node:.

We trained for 500 steps, which took about 2 hours on 64 H100s, at about 8,000 tokens per second. Mean token accuracy rose from 72% to 84% and the loss fell from 1.26 to 0.57, which signals a good fine-tuning run.

Muse Spark Open is a coding and agentic model. We wanted to see that for ourselves, so we tried a mixture of multi-modal and agentic tasks that use the model's image and audio inputs. Everything below is something you can run or fork.

In a recent development, we combined 2-bit quantized Muse Spark open (served on llama.cpp) with the Pi coding agent to generate and iteratively improve 3D assets in Three.js. You can find the prompt here, as the model is quantized it requires a bit more steering. We get 18 TPS on llama.cpp on Mac Ultra.

It then sends those images back to the same model on llama server for visual feedback. Pi uses that feedback to edit the code and repeats the process.

In a recent development, we tested Spark on computer use tasks and were amazed by the performance, so we have built a lean demo that also serves to teach you how a computer use agent works. You can also further customize this for your needs. This is both an educational example and something you can run in a few lines. You can find it here.

Muse Spark NVFP4 Browser Agent with OpenEnv and HF Sandboxes.

where the remote sandbox contains the environment and the browser as illustrated below.

Muse Spark Open sees the previous actions, system prompt, url and the screenshot of the browser to take an action, and nothing else (no DOM, no HTML code, nothing) so it’s a truly multimodal browser demo.

Finally, we wanted to push Spark’s agentic multimodality to the limits, so we set up this space that combines the model’s audio, image, and agentic properties into a browser agent. We give the model a general description of a thing we need and it interacts with the integrated browser to find options on Amazon.

Muse Spark Open takes the voice input and reasons over the type of product that meets the descriptions, searches for it on Amazon, and selects the most appropriate based on criteria.

OpenAI and Cisco introduce Shirudo

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An open-source runtime that helps operators protect running Linux systems without needing to wait for the patch or restarts.
  • OpenAI and Cisco are launching Shirudo, an open-source runtime that helps teams protect Linux systems while they roll out patches.
  • Recent findings suggest that we’re inviting developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators across the industry to help develop the project further.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An open-source runtime that helps operators protect running Linux systems without needing to wait for the patch or restarts.

OpenAI and Cisco are launching Shirudo, an open-source runtime that helps teams protect Linux systems while they roll out patches. In a controlled test⁠(opens in a newly introduced window), a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart.

Recent findings suggest that we’re inviting developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators across the industry to help develop the project further. The project brings together OpenAI’s frontier AI, security and infrastructure research and Cisco’s infrastructure and security expertise to help protect the systems people rely on every day.

Sources indicate that testing and deploying a patch can still take days or weeks. Protecting a service in the meantime can be challenging because an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same Linux operation. Blocking that operation entirely could take the service offline.

Shirudo (Japanese for “shield”) is designed to help security teams navigate this tradeoff. Teams can test whether a temporary safeguard, called a shield, blocks the behavior that exposes a vulnerability while allowing legitimate requests through. Once an operator approves the shield, it can be deployed while the service continues running.

Recent findings suggest that shirudo uses eBPF, a Linux technology that allows small programs to run at specific points inside the operating system. This makes it possible to observe suspicious activity and apply targeted security protections to running systems.

How the guardian agent observes and protects a running system with eBPF.

OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo around four core capabilities:.

Live protection: eBPF shields can block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system. Security teams can monitor how a proposed shield would affect applications before enforcing it.

Defense at machine speed: OpenAI and Cisco are designing Shirudo to give agents programmable controls to investigate vulnerabilities, develop targeted shields, and validate their effectiveness against exploits and real workloads. Security teams control what gets deployed.

In a recent development, trusted deployment: Shields are cryptographically signed and verified before loading. Linux's eBPF verifier checks eBPF programs against its safety rules, while kernel security controls restrict unauthorized changes.

Hardware-backed verification: Shirudo uses a Trusted Platform Module (TPM) to support a verifiable record of protections being loaded or removed. Operators can use this evidence to check whether systems meet their security requirements.

It has been revealed that the Shirudo technical walkthrough⁠(opens in a new window) from the Linux Plumbers Conference shows how to apply a shield and verify it on the target host⁠(opens in a new window). The Java4Shell vulnerability is another example illustrating how a targeted shield can protect a running application while a permanent patch is being prepared. Using OpenAI's Codex, the team generated a shield that added an input check to Java's Base64 decoder and attached it directly to a running Elasticsearch process. When attempting to exploit the vulnerability, the shield rejected the malicious input, blocking the attack while Elasticsearch continued running. You can read more here⁠(opens in a new window).

Shirudo is a first step toward infrastructure that can adapt to emerging threats while remaining reliable. We want to strengthen the operating system foundations needed to deploy these protections at scale, including hardening the kernel and core services, limiting workload permissions, and making updates and recovery safer.

Our long-term goal is to enable defenders and AI agents to swiftly identify affected systems, validate protections, and deploy eBPF shields that block exploits without disrupting workloads. Applications should run with only the permissions they need, governed by policies that are automatically generated and maintained.

Recent findings suggest that we will combine frontier AI with security and infrastructure research to discover vulnerabilities and test defenses against realistic attacks. We aim to make it easier for operators to detect and contain compromises, prevent attackers from moving across systems, and restore services to a verified, known-good state. Hardware-backed attestation and independent network controls provide additional assurance even if individual systems are compromised.

OpenAI and Cisco are open-sourcing Shirudo⁠(opens in a upcoming window) so developers, security researchers, and infrastructure operators can inspect the code, test protections, and contribute to its development. Shirudo is licensed under BSD 2-Clause, with its BPF programs dual-licensed under BSD and GPL.

Our goal is to make tested shields available alongside vulnerability disclosures, giving operators a way to evaluate and deploy temporary protections while preparing permanent patches.

Try Shirudo: Follow the VM quickstart⁠(opens in a latest window) to sign, load, and verify a test protection.

Get hands-on: Explore Shirudo through Isovalent's self-guided lab⁠(opens in a upcoming window).

Join the technical deep dive: Register for the December 15 webinar⁠(opens in a new window).

Industry observers note that we’re building Shirudo in the open with the people who build, run, and secure Linux systems. We welcome contributions to the runtime, fresh shields, and improvements to Linux and eBPF. If you'd like to get involved, take a look at the code on GitHub⁠(opens in a new window), read the docs⁠(opens in a new window), and let us know what you find⁠(opens in a new window).

SciFig2Data: A Workflow for Recovering Structured Data from Scientific Figures

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (181 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.31787v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scientific measurements reported in scholarly articles are often embedded in compound figures rather than available as machine-readable data. Recovering these measurements at literature scale requires an integrated workflow for figure localization, panel decomposition, chart identification, numerical reconstruction, and experimental context association. We present \textit{SciFig2Data}, an automated, high-throughput workflow for harvesting structured experimental data from scientific PDF repositories. The system integrates multi-scale document element detection, adaptive compound figure decomposition, two-stage OCR-based semantic filtering, Swin-based chart classification, and instruction-guided multimodal large language model (MLLM) reconstruction. It further incorporates directory-level batch execution, caching, and structured logging to support large-scale processing. We demonstrate the workflow on two biomedical literature corpora comprising 605 toxicology and pharmacology articles and 551 lipid nanoparticle (LNP) articles. The pipeline successfully reconstructed 468 and 242 tabular outputs from the respective corpora, illustrating its practical applicability to literature-scale scientific data harvesting. By associating reconstructed measurements with caption-derived experimental metadata, SciFig2Data provides a workflow for transforming graphical evidence in scholarly publications into structured, context-enriched data records for downstream AI4Science applications.

#38399. Frontier and Center: Why your data agents need a “wind tunnel”

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1643 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Google ↗ Open Full Page

Frontier and Center: Why your data agents need a “wind tunnel”

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1643 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that imagine you're building a data agent to answer questions about an enterprise data warehouse.
  • According to recent reports, other disciplines test differently.
  • Data agents need a wind tunnel too: a synthetic data estate (the databases, documents, and chat history where a manufacturer's knowledge lives) with the same structure and causal behavior as a real organization, while synthesizing every name, number, and document.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Software Engineer, Data Cloud Frontier AI.

Technical Lead, Data Cloud Frontier AI.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

Industry observers note that imagine you're building a data agent to answer questions about an enterprise data warehouse. Ideally, you'd develop and test it against production data, but access restrictions and data sensitivity make that difficult – especially when the engineers building the agent sit outside the team that owns the data. Even with access, a live warehouse is a poor test track: Catalog descriptions are often incomplete or contradicted by institutional knowledge in docs and chat threads; there’s no verified answer key across its thousands of tables; and you can't systematically vary the complexity of the data and documents to see where the agent breaks. So teams often test on toy datasets and hope the agent holds up in production.

According to recent reports, other disciplines test differently. Automobile designers study aerodynamics by putting a scale model in a wind tunnel, which reproduces the airflow forces that matter while ignoring surface details like paint and badges. A shape that performs well in the tunnel performs well on the road because the tunnel preserves the physical properties the shape responds to.

Data agents need a wind tunnel too: a synthetic data estate (the databases, documents, and chat history where a manufacturer's knowledge lives) with the same structure and causal behavior as a real organization, while synthesizing every name, number, and document. It is designed to preserve what the agent reasons over: how tables relate, what business events create which records, where institutional knowledge lives, and how definitions get messy. When those properties hold, an agent's behavior in the tunnel tracks its behavior on production data, even though the two share no sensitive content.

Recent findings suggest that at Google, we built an internal data simulator to serve as a wind tunnel for our enterprise data agents. Rather than copying proprietary schemas or cataloging every undocumented quirk in a live warehouse, an engineer starts with a short, plain-English description of organizational patterns, for example: "Simulate a two-plant brake manufacturer with an ERP, a shop-floor execution system, and a three-shift schedule where second-shift supervisors track downtime differently from operations and finance." From just a few sentences, the simulator invents a structurally analogous company ("Calder Brakes"), generating its schemas, rows, event history, documents, and chat threads alongside a benchmark of hard questions and a verified answer key.

Figure 1. Production data and its synthetic counterpart share causal structure without sharing sensitive content. A short description of domain patterns seeds the wind tunnel, where the agent is evaluated over read-only tools and behavioral trends carry back to production.

Why did we do this? Most data agents are evaluated on small, clean test databases with well-labeled tables, unambiguous metrics, and no conflicting documents. Those datasets are convenient, but they rarely test the judgment that enterprise data demands.

Once generated, a synthetic estate is served through a read-only interface — SQL execution, schema browsing, and document search — that any agent can call without seeing the blueprint or answer key. But consider what happens when an agent is asked either a qualitative onboarding question or a quantitative metric question from our simulated factory, "Calder Brakes Plant 2":.

In a recent development, qualitative: "A newly introduced analyst is joining the team. What should they know about how 'downtime' is handled here, before they start producing reports?".

Recent findings suggest that A naive agent falls into the same trap on both questions. It searches for the most authoritative document and finds a policy memo from Bob, a second-shift supervisor, which states that downtime means unplanned stoppages only, and planned changeovers don't count. Bob is confident, articulate, and senior, so the agent summarizes his definition — and filters out planned changeovers when writing its SQL query.

Both answers are wrong. In fact, the plant's official metric counts changeovers as planned downtime. Bob sincerely believes his version because it flatters his shift's numbers, but weeks later the metric owner quietly corrects the record in a follow-up thread. Getting either question right requires looking past a document's tone, checking who owns the metric before writing SQL, and tracing later corrections. This is where data agents often fail in production.

A synthetic estate is only useful for evaluation if its answer key is accurate and reproducible. Our simulator achieves this by separating simulated tech giant’s design from data generation across four stages (Figure 2).

According to recent reports, figure 2. One pipeline, one source of truth. In the estate-generation pipeline, only ① Compile blueprint invents facts and ③ Render documents phrases those fixed facts as prose (blue boxes); ② Simulate & build tables (plus SQL answer computation) runs deterministically from the frozen blueprint and seed, before ④ Evaluate agent tests the agent over read-only tools.

First, the Compile blueprint stage uses a language model to turn the pattern prompt into a frozen blueprint specifying the company's systems, people, metrics, and individual beliefs. Those beliefs can be mistaken on purpose — Bob's flawed definition of downtime is recorded alongside the official metric, planting the trap and its solution together.

In the estate-generation pipeline, Compile blueprint is the only point where a language model decides what is true. Once the blueprint is frozen, Simulate & build tables runs deterministically without a model: employees act on their schedules, triggering tickets, shift handovers, and database rows, so that every record traces back to the event that created it. Organizational messiness emerges naturally from this timeline, such as outdated procedures or conflicting definitions, while row-level flaws that model real ingestion glitches (e.g., retry-storm duplicate rows, unmerged keys, or a mid-quarter unit change) are injected into the tables. Every flaw is recorded in a machine-readable messiness log so the benchmark generator can adjust the ground-truth SQL queries to account for the messy tables.

It has been revealed that given the same blueprint and random seed, the simulator produces identical tables and an identical SQL answer key on every run. The only subsequent step in building the estate that calls a model is Render documents, which turns the facts fixed in the blueprint into memos and chat threads in each person's writing style. Finally, Evaluate agent tests the agent over read-only tools.

Three build-time checks keep the benchmark honest:.

Computed SQL and rubric gold answers: Every quantitative question ships with the SQL query that computes its expected ("gold") answer against the messy tables. Because the messiness log records injected retry duplicates on defect rows, the benchmark generator automatically pairs a defect-count question with the deduplicating COUNT(DISTINCT) query (240) – and runs decoy SQL queries representing common mistakes (like an un-deduplicated COUNT(*) or Bob's changeover filter) to verify that falling for a trap yields a different number. Qualitative questions ship with a rubric grounded in the blueprint's metric owner, official definition, and correction trail. If the estate lacks the data to verify a question, the generator drops the item rather than shipping an unverified question.

Verified documents: Every rendered memo and chat thread is checked against the blueprint to confirm it states its assigned facts without introducing unrecorded numbers, dates, or names.

Hallucination sentinels: The simulator plants questions about invented metrics like "Basalt Velocity Ratio" that appear nowhere in the estate; a reliable agent abstains and reports that no such metric exists.

A wind tunnel does not need to match the exact score an agent gets on production data; it needs to reproduce the same behavioral trends: direction (if longer reasoning chains lower accuracy on real data, they should lower accuracy in the tunnel) and rate (accuracy should degrade at the similar pace as contradictions accumulate). When those trends hold, you can confidently compare agent versions and dial up complexity step by step to find where reasoning breaks down.

We test how closely our simulated estates match reality — and whether evaluation signals carry over — at three levels:.

In a recent development, our simulator builds on two research threads. In database question answering, benchmarks like BIRD and Spider 2.0 have moved from clean schemas to messy databases, while agent environments like WebArena, tool-use benchmarks like τ-bench, and Generative Agents simulate websites or use language models to role-play human users. In contrast, our simulator's employees follow deterministic rules tied to their roles and schedules, so a single seed replays the exact same organizational history every time.

We also adapt an intuition from domain randomization in robotics, where simulations vary surface details like lighting and textures during training while keeping the underlying physics faithful. Applied to data agent evaluation, that means synthesizing every surface name, number, and document from a short pattern description, while keeping the causal structure, cross-document links, and institutional messiness faithful to enterprise reality.

Sources indicate that generating a test estate on demand removes a bottleneck between enterprises that own sensitive data, and the engineering teams building data agents for them. Traditionally, developing and benchmarking an enterprise agent required access to production tables and a hand-labeled question set — the two assets hardest to share across organizational or compliance boundaries. We use this wind tunnel internally to stress-test and harden Google Cloud's data agents against realistic enterprise messiness without touching customer data, and the same blueprint-first architecture can be applied by any engineering team building evaluation suites for their own agents.

Synthetic evaluation still carries two risks: overfitting to the simulator's patterns of messiness, and drift as a live business evolves away from its blueprint. The discipline required is the same one that wind-tunnel engineers practice: Periodically calibrate the tunnel against real-world runs, keep benchmark difficulty aligned with production failure modes, and treat the simulation as a living model. Your agents — and their customers — will thank you.

Today, AWS reveals that AWS Quick, the AI workspace for business consumers, now supports Japanese, German, Vietnamese, and Chinese (Simplified and Traditional). AWS Quick now displays its interface in these languages and responds in the language each user chooses. Teams that work primarily in these languages can now use AWS Quick without switching to English.

Sources indicate that for example, a finance team in Japan can ask questions about their business data in Japanese and get answers in Japanese, and a marketing team in Germany can create research reports in German. Language support covers chat, research reports, and apps in the AWS Quick web app, the desktop app for macOS and Windows, and the mobile app for iOS and Android.

Support for these languages is available in all AWS Regions where AWS Quick is available.

To get started, open Settings in AWS Quick, choose Appearance and Language, and select your language. To learn more, see the AWS Quick product page.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

Apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

The full Apertus 1.5 training pipeline.

We introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:.

Overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All newly introduced data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

Alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

It has been revealed that the multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

While still trailing frontier open-weight models, the new release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

In a recent development, we also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 reveals strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

Apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

Industry observers note that the results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

Recent findings suggest that all recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

The report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

Proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

According to recent reports, access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been confirmed by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

In a recent development, thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team declared the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

It has been revealed that in summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

If you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

It has been revealed that project Apertus, et al. “Apertus 1.5: From Open Text Models to Open Multimodal Reasoners.” arXiv:2610.15542. Preprint, arXiv, October 11, 2026. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2610.15542.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • AWS Network Firewall is a stateful, managed, network firewall and intrusion detection and prevention service for your VPC.

In a recent development, AWS Network Firewall introduces the public preview of automated internet firewall (Preview), a latest centralized control that allows you to configure Network Firewall, with native network address translation (NAT) capability, on the internet gateways of all the Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs) in your environment. Using automated internet firewall (Preview) mode, you can centrally define your Network Firewall security rules and enforce them on all inbound and outbound traffic across the internet gateways of your VPCs. You are not required to make routing or architectural changes to deploy automated internet firewall (Preview). You can deploy it across select VPCs or your entire account, organization or organization unit.

AWS Network Firewall is a stateful, managed, network firewall and intrusion detection and prevention service for your VPC. Customers use it to inspect their traffic and secure AWS resources. Prior to this launch, customers would configure AWS Network Firewalls inside their VPCs in the traffic path of all internet communication to achieve thorough security coverage against the threats on the internet. They deployed Network Firewall endpoints in dedicated subnets and made route updates for every subnet that needed internet access across all their VPCs. In addition, they monitored the environment to ensure that no upcoming internet network paths bypassed these security controls. Automated internet firewall (Preview) makes this deployment and management simpler. You just define and maintain filtering rules, and AWS enforces it directly at the internet gateway of every VPC in scope, ensuring that all intended traffic entering or leaving your VPCs via the internet gateway is inspected. Automated Internet firewall comes with built-in NAT functionality for your egress-only internet connectivity needs. You can use it to filter traffic, perform NAT and log all internet activity across all internet gateways. You don't need to make architectural changes inside every VPC or monitor every internet network path. Automated Internet firewall (Preview) allows you the option to automatically extend your organization's security policy to all future VPCs and subnets at creation.

To help you get started promptly, automated internet firewall comes with a default security policy, which uses Amazon managed rule groups including active threat defense that uses AWS unique threat intelligence to protect your workloads against evolving threats on the internet. You can also create your own custom rule groups or use any of the managed rule groups from AWS Marketplace with automated internet firewall.

It has been revealed that AWS Network Firewall operating in automated internet firewall mode (Preview) is available in preview in all AWS Regions except MXP, AWS GovCloud, and China. To learn more, visit the Network Firewall documentation and see the AWS Network Firewall pricing page. To get started, visit the Amazon VPC or Network Security Manager console.

TACT-Bench: Testing Adaptive Conversational Threats against Tool-Use Agents

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (245 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.31756v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The growing autonomy of AI agents in using external tools and making decisions has created an urgent need for comprehensive safety benchmarks. Existing benchmarks test compromised tool channels or adaptive multi-turn attacks, though they may not capture the unique capabilities of policy-governed tool-use agents, which must resist unauthorized requests without abandoning the legitimate work embedded in the same interaction. To fill this gap, we introduce TACT-Bench, a stateful benchmark built around scenario-specific stories, personas, manipulation tactics, and response-adaptive escalation. Each adversarial task targets an action explicitly prohibited by the policy provided to the assistant, while the policy remains hidden from the attacking user. TACT pairs each adversarial task with at least one benign counterpart, and its adversarial tasks retain authorized ground-truth actions when a compliant resolution remains available. We define these base tasks as TACT-Base. We additionally introduce TACT-TrustPrime, which places an independent benign task before an unrelated attack in the same conversation. We also propose Paired Selective Trustworthiness (PST), which combines explicit safe refusal with demonstrated capability on matched benign tasks, to analyze an agent's overcautiousness and practicality. Averaged across 6 different models as assistants, TACT-Base raises Attack-Induced Failure Rate (AFR) by 17.53% over four compatible attack baselines, and TACT-TrustPrime raises it by a further 17.01%. The two evaluated defense methods reduce AFR by only 8.35%--9.41% on average and do not consistently improve PST, underscoring the need for stronger policy-enforcement methods.

Clay⁠(opens in a new window) is a self-learning revenue engine designed to help. Using GPT‑6 Astra, GPT‑6 Sol, and other models, Clay enables users to build lists of companies and people, enrich those records using agents, and use that information in go-to-market plays.

Clay also brings these capabilities to where customers are already working with plugins for Codex and ChatGPT, making it easier to create and run go-to-market workflows and research accounts and deals.

In a recent development, “Clay in ChatGPT gives sales reps a way to understand more about the customers they’re trying to sell to. It brings all of that rich context to the places they’re already working.”.

Clay’s Codex integration lets builders create and run go-to-market plays in Codex, while giving sales reps access to data they can use to research an account or understand a deal they’re trying to close.

Jeff has seen reps combine information from their own systems and public datasets to determine how to best communicate their product’s value to a customer. “Customers love using Codex for a lot of different tasks in sales,” he says. “We’ve seen the best sales reps be the most empowered by this.”.

Clay’s ChatGPT plugin brings the same customer data into another tool reps already use, helping them learn more about prospects without leaving ChatGPT. Jeff says, “It’s been a substantial success.”.

OpenAI models power Claygent’s research, qualification, enrichment, and signal detection, as well as the agent that helps consumers build workflows and coordinate other Clay agents.

Clay uses GPT‑6 Sol as its primary model, with GPT‑6 Astra for harder tasks and GPT‑6 Luna for cost-sensitive work. That range supports background research and copywriting as well as agents that users work with directly.

The Responses API lets Clay use different levels of intelligence and cost through the same interface. “Having the same Responses API across the different price points is something that’s super appealing to us with OpenAI models,” noted Jeff.

GPT‑6 Astra also helps Jeff build and test software. He used to spend much of his time manually checking features he had built; now he can ask GPT‑6 Astra to handle more of that work.

It has been revealed that he explains, “GPT‑6 Astra really changed how I build software because it fully closed the loop on the engineering process. Now I can have Astra write code, add tests, and then actually run the tests and test the feature and record that and upload that in the PR. It simplifies my life a lot.”.

In a recent development, for Clay’s customers, Jeff sees GPT‑Live‑1 as a way to use Clay and Codex by voice and help prospects learn about a product. Clay is working on inbound sales development features that would let an agent show a product or service to a prospect. He also sees the Decisions API as another way to integrate models into Clay and open up newly introduced use cases.

Clay’s ambition is to carry go-to-market workflows from start to finish, with agents that improve as they learn from the results. For Jeff, the goal is to empower builders “to bring the same shift that happened in software engineering to go-to-market.”.
